articles.body:
Thanks for following the blog tonight. The election has ended without a clear winner. Here are the top news lines from what will go down as one of New Zealand’s closest elections in many decades.

Christopher Luxon’s National party and its right-leaning coalition partners are on the brink of a wafer-thin majority that could allow it to eke out a return to power.

The left-wing bloc, led by Labour’s Chris Hipkins, fell short of a majority.

Neither Luxon or Hipkins claimed victory or conceded defeat. Both acknowledged an expected wait before a governing coalition is negotiated.

A centrist newcomer, the Opportunity party, have entered parliament, polling above the 5% threshold. They could potentially be a kingmaker in a coalition.

Final results are expected on 27 November. Coalition talks will likely take weeks.

Hundreds of thousands of special votes are yet to be counted and could change the shape of parliament.

Saturday figures showed there could be a 130-seat parliament, with 66 seats needed for a majority.

Results suggested a coalition of National, Act and NZ First would hold 67 seats.

The 67 included 42 for National, 13 for Act and 12 for NZ First.

The left-bloc totalled 56 seats: Labour 35, Greens 16 and 5 for Te Pāti Māori.

Over the coming days and weeks we will get a sense of the magnitude of Qiulae Wong and the Opportunity party’s success tonight. Opportunity are currently projected to claim seven seats in parliament.

Wong has said that if she held the tiebreaker power, she was open to negotiating with either a conservative or a left-wing government and would deal first with whichever major party won the most votes.

The right-wing bloc might not need her, and Luxon has ruled out governing with Opportunity. Analysts say, however, that both major party leaders would likely answer the phone if Wong held the only path to power.

You can elle Duff.

With 0.56% support, Te Pāti Māori will be stoked with its result tonight, writes Jamie Tahana.

It seems odd, but the Māori party has spent the election deliberately asking people not to give them their party vote. Instead, they asked for electorate votes only.

Just a reminder, seven of the seats in New Zealand’s parliament are reserved for representatives of Māori voters – you can

The party’s co-leaders, Rawiri Waititi and Debbie Ngarewa-Packer, have comfortably won their respective seats of Waiariki and Te Tai Hauauru; Oriini Kaipara swept the Auckland seat of Tamaki Makaurau; Hana Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke, who hit international stardom for her haka in parliament, has cruised across the line in Hauraki-Waikato; while Aperahama Edwards holds a narrow lead over the Greens’ Hūhana Lydon in the far North seat of Te Tai Tokerau.

That’s five seats. But with a party vote so low, they will be five overhang seats.

Still, after a term that has seen plenty of in-fighting in Te Pāti Māori, there are signs of frustration in the Māori electorate, with Waititi and Ngarewa-Packer seeing significantly reduced majorities.

The Greens have fallen short of gaining their first ever Māori electorate, but across the seats party vote has risen to about 40%, making the party a significant force in Māori politics.

Labour, having been punished by the Māori electorate in 2023, has improved, particularly in terms of party vote, and has claimed a new MP in Mananui Ramsden, who won the country’s largest electorate, Te Tai Tonga.

So, hundreds of thousands of special votes are going to potentially change where things stand right now.

In his speech tonight, Luxon said 300,000 special votes were yet to be counted. Those votes, which will be counted and known by 27 November, typically sway left.

In the 2023 election there 600,000 special votes, and National dropped from 50 seats in the preliminary count to 48 seats.

In a 130-seat parliament, in which 66 seats are needed to govern, this is where things stand with 97% of the vote counted. However, special votes are still to be counted and the lay of the land will not be clear until 27 November.

Jamie Tahana has this hot-take on the Luxon speech:

It was a tough line to tread for a speech: National is the biggest party on current results – 29.30% – but Luxon has also led the party to one of its most unpopular points, only 0.1% ahead of Labour. Luxon has also lost some of his most senior and experienced MPs, which he conceded required “some tough phone calls”.

Luxon said, that because of the closeness of the result, and with special votes still to be counted, caretaker conventions will apply.

“For now, I want to tell New Zealanders that well established caretaker conventions apply … The daily business of government will continue.”

Caretaker convention basically means that while a new government is being formed, the incumbent government is in “caretaker” mode, which means it will carry on the normal business of governing.

Jamie Tahana notes that for Luxon to continue as prime minister, he will have to cobble together a three- or four-party coalition, from a weakened position compared to 2023.

In his speech, Luxon said: “Negotiations and compromises are going to be required … A number of races are still too close to call.”

Luxon called the election “too close to call”, and said “meaningful negotiations” for a new coalition government will start after the final results are known on 27 November.

“It looks like an MMP special,” he said. “It’s heartening to see that so far National is once again the largest party in parliament and we have a path to forming the next government.”

Luxon arrived to a crowd of about 700 raucous supporters chanting “three more years”. He was flanked by his wife Amanda and two children, waved and grinned as he descended a stairwell flanked in blue light.

A heavy music track - which could not be immediately identified through Shazam - thrummed as he walked down a long aisle, hugging supporters.

When he took the podium, Luxon conceded the election was “too close to call” but the crowd cheered as he announced National had secured the highest party count.

He went on to acknowledge Labour leader Chris Hipkins, and admonished supporters who booed Quilae Wong and Opportunity, saying it was “not the kiwi way”.

Luxon is also paying tribute to those high-ranking National MPs who find themselves out of a job tonight: Nicola Willis, Paul Goldsmith and Gerry Brownlee. “I want to thank you … for your years of service to our party”.

articles.title: Four things we learned this week about 2028 White House race
articles.summary: The seismic Democratic gains in Congress could shape the presidential election, so who had a good night and who's making moves?
articles.preview: Ballots are still being counted in the US midterm elections but the political landscape is already pivoting to the 2028 White House race. Buoyed by major gains in Congress, Democrats will have momentum as they prepare for the contest to succeed President Donald Trump. But a good showing in the midterms does not guarantee a White House win two years later. Barack Obama was re-elected in 2012 despite huge Republican gains in 2010. No one has yet entered the presidential race but potential candidates will be preparing behind the scenes.
articles.body:
Ballots are still being counted in the US midterm elections but the political landscape is already pivoting to the 2028 White House race.

Buoyed by major gains in Congress, Democrats will have momentum as they prepare for the contest to succeed President Donald Trump.

But a good showing in the midterms does not guarantee a White House win two years later. Barack Obama was re-elected in 2012 despite huge Republican gains in 2010.

No one has yet entered the presidential race but potential candidates will be preparing behind the scenes.

Vice-President's JD Vance's reflection on where the midterms went wrong for Republicans has been interpreted as him paving the way for a 2028 run.

The results of Tuesday's election and the historic size of Democratic gains could shape the White House race in several ways. Here are four takeaways.

1. Big winners in the midterms now have momentum

Several prominent potential presidential candidates were running in the 2026 midterms - and some emerged looking strong.

Georgia Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff won by a sizeable margin in the politically competitive state that Trump won in 2024.

While he has previously said he has no plans to run for president, his successful campaign, with several viral moments, helped boost his national profile.

Another potential Democratic nominee, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, swept aside his Republican challenger.

Shapiro has not committed to a 2028 run but analysts point to his broad appeal in swing-state Pennsylvania as a sign that he could be competitive on the national stage.

Illinois Governor JB Pritzker also won after a campaign pundits in his state described as a "tune-up" for a presidential run.

California Governor Gavin Newsom could not run for re-election in the midterms but he is invested in the outcome of a ballot initiative to tax the state's wealthy residents which he campaigned against.

On the Republican side, there were two potential 2028 names running in Arkansas.

Republican Senator Tom Cotton and Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders - a one-time Trump administration press secretary - were able to stay in office by a narrower margin than before, both earning just above half of the votes in the conservative state.

- Trump names Stephen Miller as new chief of staff

- Published17 hours ago

- What Democrats can and can't do with their new power after taking Congress

- Published2 days ago

2. JD Vance and Trump's allies under pressure

Exit polls suggest the swing against Republicans was partly due to anger felt by voters at the actions of the Trump administration.

That could present a challenge to his potential successors who come from the ranks of the current leadership, including Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

"The one person who has been hurt badly by this election campaign is Vance," said Karen Beckwith, a professor of political science at Case Western Reserve University in Ohio.

Vance has already sought to distance himself from defeat - and from a foreign policy adventure in Iran that was politically disastrous for his party.

"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote on X.

Rubio has denied reports he is considering leaving his post ahead of a 2028 presidential run.

Other possible Republican candidates may benefit from not being part of the administration. Some have been staking out a position on what went wrong and what next.

In a lengthy post on X, Senator Ted Cruz, who was not running this year, said that too many Republican politicians seem like "they didn't care" about the economic issues faced by voters.

"It is dark right now, but it is always darkest before the dawn, and morning is coming," he wrote. "That is my fervent prayer, and that is my commitment to you."

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who abandoned his 2024 presidential run after being trounced by Trump early on, was similarly critical and pointed to Republican victories in Florida as a sign of what can be accomplished.

Former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie was blunt in his assessment: "The Trump era is over."

3. Left and centre Democrats in fight for future

Both the centrist and left wings of the Democratic Party have claimed victory from the results as each side sifts through possible 2028 contenders.

Dozens are already making moves, Obama's former adviser Jim Messina has told the BBC.

El-Sayed's win in Michigan was a breakthrough moment for left-wing Democrats because he triumphed in a swing state.

His supporters now claim his win could supercharge left-wing candidates in the 2028 election.

"The old notions of electability are out the door, and bold economist populist outsiders proved they can win in battleground states," said Adam Green, the co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee.

Green added that the "water is now warm" for candidates such as New York Democratic representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run in presidential primaries and "know that they can win."

Moderate Democrats, however, claimed victories across the country, with the "Blue Dog Caucus" of moderate and conservative Democrats gaining at least 14 seats in Congress, nearly doubling its current size.

This has led many within that wing of the party to conclude that centrist candidates that bill themselves as pragmatic and willing to work with conservatives could woo Republican voters.

Given the success of Democratic candidates who focused on cost of living issues, an economy-first approach will likely be a focus again in two years.

Amirah Siquierah, the director of federal affairs at the Working Families Party, said successful candidates in 2028 will combine economic populism with newer concerns such as data centres.

- Dozens of Democrats eyeing 2028 presidential run, says former Obama aide

- Published21 hours ago

4. Support of Hispanic voters must be earned

Both parties must contend with a changing political map and a shifting coalition of support for 2028.

Once "safe" Republican parts of the country can no longer be considered conservative strongholds.

Texas is left with only one Republican at a statewide level, which means its 40 electoral college votes could be up for grabs in 2028.

Christina Pascucci, a political commentator and one-time Senate candidate in California, said the midterms "challenge long-held political assumptions" and show that "neither party can afford to take its traditional strongholds for granted".

That is true of both Democrats and Republicans who will need to win over swing voters, added Pascucci, now the CEO of Atlas Global, a global communications and advisory firm.

"Neither party owns these voters," she said.

The Trump coalition of working class and Latino voters faltered, reversing many of the gains he had made with those electorates in his successful 2024 campaign.

Driena Sixto, a former spokesperson for Turning Point USA and a conservative political commentator, told the BBC that she believed that Republicans will have to change their messaging to Latino voters ahead of 2028 for any future candidate to be able to reverse the trend.

"Last time, the campaign message was one of safe communities and fighting back against trafficking," she said.

"After the president was sworn in, I think a lot of messaging from the White House did too much to highlight deportations. That was the divide."

articles.title: Rains flood 70,000 displaced families’ tents in Gaza
articles.summary: Initial losses are estimated at about $3m, according to Gaza's Government Media Office.
articles.preview: Initial losses are estimated at about $3m, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office. About 70,000 tents sheltering displaced Palestinians have been flooded in the Gaza Strip within 12 hours of the first winter storm of the season, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office. In a statement on Saturday, the office said initial losses were estimated at about $3m. Dozens of walls had collapsed and people had been injured, it said, while cracked buildings at risk of collapse posed a growing danger.
articles.body:
Initial losses are estimated at about $3m, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office.

About 70,000 tents sheltering displaced Palestinians have been flooded in the Gaza Strip within 12 hours of the first winter storm of the season, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office.

In a statement on Saturday, the office said initial losses were estimated at about $3m. Dozens of walls had collapsed and people had been injured, it said, while cracked buildings at risk of collapse posed a growing danger.

The office held Israel “fully responsible” for what it called a disaster caused by the continued closure of crossings and the blocking of shelter and reconstruction materials. It urged the international community and UN agencies to intervene immediately to protect the displaced.

Gaza’s civil defence agency said its crews received about 1,500 distress calls in just 10 hours after the rain began early on Saturday, with water levels in several shelter sites rising by 30-40cm (12-16 inches).

“What we feared has actually happened,” civil defence spokesman Mahmoud Basal told Al Jazeera. “A few shelter centres were completely flooded, and everyone inside them has now been forced out into the unknown.”

Basal said premature babies, the elderly and the sick were most at risk. “Those living in tents are at risk of death at any moment, and of illness at any moment,” he said.

The storm also brought down buildings damaged in Israel’s genocidal war on the enclave that began in October 2023.

The civil defence agency said rescuers had evacuated residents of a building in the central Nuseirat area that partially collapsed in the strong winds and rain. In northern Gaza, the wall of a separate building fell down due to heavy rainfall, injuring two people, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa.

Footage from camps in Gaza City, Khan Younis and Deir el-Balah showed families wading through ankle-deep water, mattresses and blankets soaked, and children standing barefoot in pools of mud and sewage.

“Even houses can’t hold up against this rain, so how can open plastic sheeting?” said Al Jazeera’s Nour Khaled, reporting from a camp in Gaza City. She said more than 28,000 widows were among those facing the winter alone with their children.

In al-Mawasi, the coastal area where more than 900,000 displaced people are sheltering in southern Gaza, rain had been falling since 10pm (20:00 GMT) on Friday, Al Jazeera’s Rami Abu Taima reported from Khan Younis.

“People woke up to find hundreds, even thousands, of tents flooded across the Gaza Strip,” he said. He added that more than 125,000 families living along the coast were at particular risk of having their tents swept away by the sea.

Gaza’s emergency committee said more than one million displaced people face a harsh winter, and that the territory urgently needs about 200,000 tents along with heating supplies.

Raed al-Dahshan, director of civil defence in Gaza, told Al Jazeera that crews could do little once they reached flooded families. “Civil defence does not have a single tarpaulin or a single tent,” he said. “We deal only with saving lives, and that is not enough.”

Aid groups blame Israeli restrictions on the entry of shelter materials.

The storm also hit Gaza’s battered health system. Mohammed Abu Salmiya, director of al-Shifa Medical Complex in Gaza City, told Al Jazeera that the hospital’s emergency department flooded and was out of service for about four hours. He warned of a rise in gastrointestinal, respiratory and skin infections as sewage mixed with rainwater inside tents.

“We will see many deaths, in the dozens and perhaps the hundreds, among newborns who need warmth in these tents,” he said.

Reporting from Gaza City port, Al Jazeera’s Ghazi al-Aloul said thousands of families had pitched tents along the shoreline, where they face strong winds and rising tides. “These tents will flood first from the rain, and second from seawater,” he said.

Many of the tents were put up in the first year of displacement and are now in their fourth, patched and re-stitched by their owners. Under the ceasefire’s humanitarian protocol, they were supposed to be replaced with caravans, which Israel has not allowed into the territory.

One displaced man on the beach told Al Jazeera: “They pushed us west towards the sea. Why don’t they just throw us into the sea and be done with it?”

Mohammed Salha, director of the Palestinian NGO Network, told Al Jazeera that only 180 to 200 trucks were entering Gaza daily, far short of the 600 agreed under the humanitarian protocol of the “ceasefire”, and that only about 40 of those carried humanitarian aid.

“We don’t want to respond after the tents flood,” Salha said, adding that 50,000 tents had been waiting on the Egyptian side of the border. “We must respond before the disaster happens.”

He described international pressure on Israel to allow in more supplies as “timid”.

articles.title: Paraguay VP Alliana sworn is as president after predecessor impeached
articles.summary: Former Paraguayan Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as president Friday to serve out the term of his predecessor, Santiago Peña, who was impeached earlier the same day for misconduct in office.
articles.preview: Paraguay Former Paraguayan Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as president Friday to serve out the term of his predecessor, Santiago Peña, who was impeached earlier the same day for misconduct in office. Alliana was elected vice president of Paraguay as Peña's running mate in 2023. He should now serve out Peña's term, which runs until August 2028. In a unanimous vote, the 44 senators present voted to remove Peña for misconduct in office, bringing a dramatic end to one of South America's most stable presidencies.
articles.body:
Paraguay

Former Paraguayan Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as president Friday to serve out the term of his predecessor, Santiago Peña, who was impeached earlier the same day for misconduct in office.

Alliana was elected vice president of Paraguay as Peña's running mate in 2023. He should now serve out Peña's term, which runs until August 2028.

In a unanimous vote, the 44 senators present voted to remove Peña for misconduct in office, bringing a dramatic end to one of South America's most stable presidencies.

The verdict came just three days after regulators seized Ueno Bank, cutting nearly 3 million customers off from their savings and bank cards and setting off a political crisis.

Ousted Paraguayan President Santiago Peña was placed under house arrest Friday on suspicion of breach of trust, shortly after the Senate removed him from office over the collapse of a major bank tied to his government.

Prosecutors ordered that Peña be held at his home until he can be brought before their economic crimes and anti-corruption unit, according to a letter to the national police commander.

The attorney general's office confirmed to The Associated Press that he had been detained there.

The order also called for the arrest of Carlos Carvallo, the former central bank chief Peña appointed. It was not immediately clear whether Carvallo was in custody.

Lawmakers accused Peña of using his political influence to steer hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds into Ueno while regulators overlooked risky insider lending.

Peña has denied wrongdoing.

A veteran of the long-ruling conservative Colorado party, Alliana, 52, is a former governor of the southern province of Ñeembucú and a former speaker of the lower house.

He has not escaped the scandal entirely: Prosecutors are also investigating him, and on Thursday lawmakers shelved an opposition bid to impeach him.

Peña had submitted his resignation Thursday, but Congress did not accept it. His lawyers, Ricardo Preda and Adolfo Ferreiro, argued that lawmakers should have approved his departure instead of pressing ahead with the impeachment trial.

Public outrage has become more thunderous by the day.

As senators deliberated Friday, crowds of protesters demanding their frozen savings back and accountability for Ueno's failure marched through downtown Asunción.

articles.title: Ukraine: Russia hits Kyiv with airstrikes ahead of trilateral talks
articles.summary: The strikes hit a major bridge and energy facilities in the Kyiv region. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Moscow of trying to "push" Ukraine "into a blackout" ahead of talks in Abu Dhabi.
articles.preview: November 7, 2026 The strikes hit a major bridge and energy facilities in the Kyiv region. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Moscow of trying to "push" Ukraine "into a blackout" ahead of talks in Abu Dhabi. Russia launched strikes on Kyiv and surrounding areas overnight, Russian and Ukrainian authorities said on Saturday. Russia's Defense Ministry said the strikes hit the Northern Bridge and the Meridian Plant.
articles.body:
November 7, 2026

The strikes hit a major bridge and energy facilities in the Kyiv region. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Moscow of trying to "push" Ukraine "into a blackout" ahead of talks in Abu Dhabi.

Russia launched strikes on Kyiv and surrounding areas overnight, Russian and Ukrainian authorities said on Saturday.

Russia's Defense Ministry said the strikes hit the Northern Bridge and the Meridian Plant.

Moscow said that the bridge was being used by the Ukrainian military to transport weapons and military equipment, while the plant is used to produce Flamingo cruise missiles.

It said the strikes damaged several energy and industrial facilities in the Kyiv region, as well as an electricity substation in the neighboring Zhytomyr region and a cargo vessel in the Black Sea.

What have Ukrainian authorities said about the attacks?

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko confirmed the strikes on the Northern Bridge, adding that the Ukrainian capital found itself in an "extremely difficult" situation regarding power, heating and water supplies. Overnight temperatures dropped to 0 degrees Celsius (32 degrees Fahrenheit) in the city.

The Kyiv region's governor, Tymur Tkachenko, said energy facilities in three of its districts had been hit.

Ukrainian authorities said that one person was killed and eight were wounded in the overnight attack.

In a statement on social media, president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Russia used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles during the attack.

He said that Russia was trying to "push Kyiv … and the entire country into a blackout" and repeated his call for increased support from the United States.

Russia has stepped up airstrikes on Ukraine in recent months, targeting energy infrastructure and major cities, and more recently hitting bridges.

Strikes come ahead of Russia-Ukraine talks

The strikes come days before a fourth round of trilateral talks between Kyiv, Moscow and Washington in Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates.

Previous rounds of US-brokered talks have failed to achieve any breakthroughs, with territorial and security questions remaining major points of contention.

On Friday, US President Donald Trump said the war could be close to being settled and that he envisioned a "big, beautiful agreement" with Moscow that involves "all of Europe."

Last Friday, a six-day local ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in the southern Kherson region enabled the evacuation of some 800 residents.

The brief truce was brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump.

articles.title: Amid protests, France's rising debt costs threaten stability
articles.summary: France plans to spend an extra €4 billion on education amid nationwide protests. But with public debt mounting and interest costs climbing, how much fiscal room does the government have?
articles.preview: November 7, 2026 France plans to spend an extra €4 billion on education amid nationwide protests. But with public debt mounting and interest costs climbing, how much fiscal room does the government have? Deeply indebted, politically trapped in a standoff between extremes and led by a government without a parliamentary majority: These are the defining features of France's current predicament.
articles.body:
November 7, 2026

France plans to spend an extra €4 billion on education amid nationwide protests. But with public debt mounting and interest costs climbing, how much fiscal room does the government have?

Deeply indebted, politically trapped in a standoff between extremes and led by a government without a parliamentary majority: These are the defining features of France's current predicament.

If, in response to nationwide protests, the government plans to provide €4 billion ($4.48 billion) in low-interest loans to renovate schools by 2030 and allocate a further €1 billion to universities by 2029, it is promising money the state simply does not have.

France's public debt stands at around 120% of gross domestic product (GDP). By comparison, Germany's debt-to-GDP ratio is roughly 65%, despite its €600 billion investment package for infrastructure and defense.

Germany still enjoys the highest possible AAA credit rating. France, by contrast, is rated AA, A+ or Aa3, depending on the credit agency. While Germany's outlook is consistently rated as stable, several agencies have assigned France a negative outlook.

As a result, the French government must pay higher interest rates on its borrowing than Berlin. The risk premium over German government bonds, known as the spread, is now at its highest level since the financial crisis. France pays nearly 1.6 percentage points more in interest than Germany on 10-year bonds.

A barometer of France's public finances

The spread acts as a kind of "fever gauge" for bond markets, explained Friedrich Heinemann, an economist at the Leibniz Center for European Economic Research (ZEW) in Mannheim.

"This fever gauge then forces a change of course. If the spread rises too sharply, France's financing conditions come under pressure, and anyone in France who needs a loan has to pay higher interest rates. Banks then get into trouble, and the crisis escalates further," Heinemann told DW.

"This could then slide toward a financial crisis, which would finally send a clear signal to everyone: Things cannot continue like this unless you are prepared to risk a genuine economic collapse," he said.

Landry Charrier, a researcher at the University of Bonn's Center for Advanced Security, Strategic and Integration Studies, however, does not expect France's debt-fueled spending spree to end anytime soon.

"French people are aware of the country's high public debt. But debt remains an abstract concept if its consequences are barely felt in everyday life. According to INSEE [the French national statistics agency — Editor's note], 56% of the population receive more in government benefits and services than they pay in taxes and social contributions. The majority therefore have a tangible interest in maintaining the status quo," Charrier told DW.

For more than half a century, France has regularly spent more than it collects in tax revenue. The last time it balanced its national budget was in 1974.

Echoes of eurozone crisis

France last paid a similarly high-risk premium at the end of 2011, during the eurozone debt crisis. What is particularly striking is how quickly it has risen: Since June 2026, the spread over German government bonds has more than doubled.

The main driver is not so much the general level of interest rates. Rather, it's the growing risk premium investors demand in response to high debt levels, political instability, large budget deficits and the recent unrest.

The higher the interest rates, the larger the share of the national budget that must be devoted to debt servicing alone. France is expected to pay more than €79 billion in interest on its total public debt in 2026. That figure is projected to exceed €91 billion in 2027 and could reach between €125 billion and €132 billion by 2030.

These figures include the costs incurred by social security funds and local authorities. The central government's interest bill alone is currently estimated at €62.6 billion by the Agence France Tresor, a French Treasury agency.

In the coming years, France will have to refinance large amounts of outstanding bonds that were issued when interest rates were at historic lows. At the same time, the country's substantial budget deficit means it must take on additional debt.

Warning shot for Germany

The trend of rising interest costs is also affecting Germany. The ZEW's Heinemann has calculated that German interest payments are likely to increase sharply by the early 2030s.

"For the federal government alone, which has so far paid around €30 billion, the figure will triple within a few years as both debt and interest rates rise. And it won't stop there — it will exceed €90 billion. Reaching €100 billion in annual interest payments in the federal budget is then no longer far off," warned the economist.

In France, however, economic realities seem to have little impact on political debate. Both the far-right National Rally (RN) and the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) are campaigning on costly promises.

RN leader Marine Le Pen, for example, wants to reinstate the retirement age of 62 while promising €140 billion in savings. Jean-Luc Melenchon, LFI's leader, has even suggested that government bonds held by the French central bank should be "thrown into the fire."

"Nobody will ever notice they've disappeared," he has claimed.

'Fairy tales from the left and the right'

For Heinemann, this is "a good example of radical parties on both the right and the left simply telling economic fairy tales."

Their common message, he said, is that "there is a way out of this mess that requires neither fiscal consolidation nor painful cuts."

Charrier is convinced that many French people have yet to grasp the seriousness of the situation.

"The euro has made it easier for France to access cheap financing and has long softened the pressure to adjust," he pointed out.

"In the past, currency devaluations [of the French franc — Editor's note] made economic imbalances immediately felt through declining purchasing power and rising prices. Today, that warning signal is missing. This has created the illusion that necessary adjustments can be postponed indefinitely," Charrier said.

This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Political chaos in Somalia after court ruling against president's term extension
articles.summary: Somalia's political crisis is deepening, with the opposition accusing the president of sending troops to arrest the Supreme Court's chief justice after the tribunal declared an extension of his term "unlawful".
articles.preview: Somalia Mogadishu residents on Friday expressed mixed feelings after Somalia's Supreme Court ruled an extension of the president's term was "unlawful". The country is mired in a deepening political crisis, with the opposition accusing President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud of sending troops to arrest the Supreme Court's chief justice. "The Supreme Court is right and its decision is right. In the world, all people and governments abide by court decisions, and the rule of law must be respected," said Abdullahi Hassan Sheikh, a Mogadishu resident.
articles.body:
Somalia

Mogadishu residents on Friday expressed mixed feelings after Somalia's Supreme Court ruled an extension of the president's term was "unlawful".

The country is mired in a deepening political crisis, with the opposition accusing President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud of sending troops to arrest the Supreme Court's chief justice.

"The Supreme Court is right and its decision is right. In the world, all people and governments abide by court decisions, and the rule of law must be respected," said Abdullahi Hassan Sheikh, a Mogadishu resident.

"I see the court decision as wrong because, when the new constitution was being approved, the court was operational," said Mohamed Farah Ahmed.

Somalia is dealing with multiple crises, with political rivalries that have descended into violent clashes, while the government loses international support for its fight against the powerful Islamist insurgent group, Al-Shabaab.

President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud has tried to move Somalia towards fully democratic elections, replacing the clan-based system in which elders pick their representatives.

But his opponents see the reforms as a power grab, especially after the president declared a "transition period" that gave him an extra year in office when his term ended in May.

Mohamud argues he was allowed to stay in office under constitutional amendments passed by parliament, to prepare for the first nationwide democratic elections in April and May 2027.

But the Supreme Court ruled on Thursday that they should never have applied to Mohamud's current term and he should have left office in May. It called for a new agreement between political parties within 30 days, and elections to be held within 90 days.

Before the ruling had even been published, the president's office announced on Facebook that he was dismissing the chief justice, Bashe Yusuf Ahmed, and appointing a replacement, because of "concerns... about the need for an efficient and fair judiciary".

The court responded that the president had no authority to fire the judge, accusing him of trying "to obstruct the administration of justice in the constitutional case filed before the Supreme Court".

A former prime minister, Hassan Ali Khaire, told reporters that the president had "launched an assault on the Supreme Court and deployed troops to its premises" on Thursday.

"The chief justice and lawyers are being pursued in their homes for arrest, have been subjected to torture, and the court's operations have been halted," he added.

His claims could not be verified by AFP, but images published by Somali media claimed to show military forces in the court's compound.

"Somalia stands at a dangerous juncture. The dismantling of our judiciary is a direct threat to the rule of law," said Ali Khaire. "I call on all sectors of Somali society to stand up now and defend Somalia's constitutionalism."

Security crisis

Most of the opposition and regional parties boycotted the vote on amending the constitution when it went to parliament in March, and some said they were barred from attending.

Violence broke out in the capital, Mogadishu, in June as political factions clashed over the issue.

The flare-up comes at a time when Somalia is also facing a security crisis related to the long-running insurgency by the Al-Qaeda-linked Al-Shabaab group that controls swathes of the country.

International donors, frustrated by the lack of progress against the militants and the endless political chaos, have been slashing funding for the international military mission that has been ongoing for almost 20 years.

Uganda, the biggest contributor to the African Union's force, announced this week that it was pulling out all troops by the end of 2027.

Washington has cut all donations to a critical United Nations logistics mission on which the military coalition relies.

articles.title: US: Giant pandas from China make public debut at Atlanta zoo
articles.summary: Ping Ping and Fu Shuang are the first giant pandas to be housed in Zoo Atlanta after a gap of two years.
articles.preview: November 7, 2026 Ping Ping and Fu Shuang are the first giant pandas to be housed in Zoo Atlanta after a gap of two years. Two giant pandas from China have made their first public appearance at a zoo in the US city of Atlanta as a queue of visitors lined up to see the bears. In a treat for them and their fans, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang — male and female, respectively — were seen munching on bamboo at Zoo Atlanta on Friday. The six-year-old pandas arrived from China's Chengdu on September 27.
articles.body:
November 7, 2026

Ping Ping and Fu Shuang are the first giant pandas to be housed in Zoo Atlanta after a gap of two years.

Two giant pandas from China have made their first public appearance at a zoo in the US city of Atlanta as a queue of visitors lined up to see the bears.

In a treat for them and their fans, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang — male and female, respectively — were seen munching on bamboo at Zoo Atlanta on Friday.

The six-year-old pandas arrived from China's Chengdu on September 27.

The FedEx flight they traveled on was dubbed the "Panda Express."

The panda duo had spent the last few weeks getting acclimated to their habitat.

Pandas return to Atlanta

Ping Ping and Fu Shuang have taken up residence in a panda enclosure at the zoo that had been vacant since 2024.

A 25-year-long partnership that saw Atlanta host four pandas on loan since 1999 ended in the midst of strained US-China ties. Seven panda cubs that were born at the zoo during that period now live in Chengdu, China.

That arrangement has been renewed under a 10-year loan agreement following a Washington summit between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping.

China's ambassador to the US, Xie Feng, said at a press conference on Friday that the pandas' arrival "marks the renewal of a decade-long bond between China and Zoo Atlanta."

Raymond King, CEO of Zoo Atlanta, described pandas as "animals that have got a unique ability to inspire curiosity, instill passion, evoke joy, and unite people around the globe."

"This extraordinary spirit of partnership helps create a future for a species that is truly beloved the world over," he said as the two adult pandas made their debut.

China's 'panda diplomacy'

China has a history of leasing the iconic pandas to other countries in a bid to build diplomatic ties, dubbed "panda diplomacy."

Cubs born in foreign zoos are typically sent back to China.

Meanwhile, unaware of the soft power they wield, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, lounged about their new habitat on Friday.

The zoo recently renovated its panda facilities and has also ensured a long-term supply of locally grown bamboo for its newest residents.

Three US zoos now house the black-and-white mammals.

articles.title: Paraguay's president impeached and under house arrest after bank collapse
articles.summary: Santiago Peña was ousted due to a banking crisis which left millions of people unable to access their money.
articles.preview: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has been impeached and placed under house arrest after a bank collapse triggered a crisis that left more than half of the country's population without access to their accounts. Peña was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office following the collapse earlier this week of Ueno Bank, which has links to his private business interests. He had offered to step down on Thursday.
articles.body:
Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has been impeached and placed under house arrest after a bank collapse triggered a crisis that left more than half of the country's population without access to their accounts.

Peña was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office following the collapse earlier this week of Ueno Bank, which has links to his private business interests.

He had offered to step down on Thursday. Rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached Peña and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents.

Peña, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing.

The impeachment charges that led to Peña's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.

He is due to be questioned on Saturday over allegations of breach of trust, influence peddling, and misappropriation of funds, prosecutor Silvia Margarita Gonzalez Vester said.

Peña's deputy, Pedro Alliana, has been sworn in as the new interim president and promised not to "abandon" the millions of people affected by the scandal.

"Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as president until 2028.

The demise of the digital bank left more than half of Paraguay's population without access to their savings after it was seized by Paraguay's central bank.

Long lines of people trying to withdraw money from Ueno branches snaked down the streets of the capital Asuncion on Tuesday and Wednesday.

An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions, prompting public outrage particularly in the capital, Asunción.

Protests erupted across the country in response, with thousands taking to the streets on Thursday to demand their money.

Earlier demonstrations featured clashes with the police, who used tear gas and water cannons on the crowd.

Peña's impeachment passed with 44 out of 45 senators voting in favour of it. One lawmaker was absent.

"It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me," Peña said in a video posted on X announcing his resignation, adding his priority was "the peace of mind of Paraguayans who entrusted their savings to our financial system".

Afterwards, senate president Basilio Núñez said Peña was found guilty of "dereliction of duty".

Senator Rafael Filizzola said: "We are facing the biggest corruption scandal in our democratic history â a tremendous blow to the state, to private citizens, and to the country's credibility and image."

Analysts say Peña is likely to now be prosecuted over the bank's collapse.

His defence lawyer Ricardo Preda described the allegations as a "reckless accusation" that was "irresponsible and opportunistic".

articles.body:
The Democrats’ sweep of Congress may make it easier for Israel’s splintered opposition to overcome deep internal divisions and form a coalition government, by increasing the urgency of unseating Benjamin Netanyahu, who has associated himself so closely with Donald Trump’s Republicans.

But as Israel took stock of the results, there was also a sense that the elections marked a longer-term shift in US politics that will make the job of any new Israeli leader far more difficult.

The United States provides Israel with critical military and diplomatic support, so nurturing bipartisan ties was the cornerstone of foreign policy for decades. Netanyahu ripped up that commitment to throw his lot in with the Republicans in general and Trump in particular.

The opposition had always attacked his decision as ill-judged. By the end of the week, they were warning that it was positively dangerous.

“These people aren’t against Israel,” prominent opposition politician Yair Lapid said of incoming Democratic lawmakers, urging his country to rebuild bridges. “They’re mainly against Netanyahu – for them, anything connected to him is toxic.”

“The easiest thing is to scream that ‘America is lost,’ because if it’s lost, you don’t have to work. That’s just not true. Not at all.”

Lapid laid out a plan to “rebuild trust” in the US, but it perhaps did more to demonstrate the scale of the problem than reassure Israelis.

His proposal of a transatlantic charm offensive by officials of a prospective new government drew a swift and sharp rebuke from the New York congressman-elect Brad Lander.

Lander, a Democrat who is Jewish and describes himself as a liberal Zionist, was detained in the occupied West Bank last month while joining Palestinians trying to harvest olives.

“Minister Lapid: As someone who won a seat in Congress last night, and who cares about Israel: you’re not listening to what American voters – Jewish and non-Jewish – are saying,” Lander wrote in a direct response.

“We aren’t starving for a barnstorming tour. We’re hungry to see respect for international law and human rights.”

In his exchange with Lapid, Lander also highlighted the arrest of journalist Abed Abu Shehada, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, as an example of how Israel violates international law. He drew a direct link with the ICE “regime of detention without charges, based on secret evidence, designed to intimidate and chill speech” that he said was rejected by US voters.

Abu Shehada was reportedly taken from his home by 15 masked security officials in a night-time raid, without an arrest warrant. Interrogators have only questioned him about a podcast interview with a public figure, lawyers acting for Abu Shehada said.

On Friday, Lander and two other incoming Jewish members of Congress, Daniel Bliss and Scott Wiener, wrote to Israel’s ambassador to the US calling for the immediate release of Abu Shehada.

“Detaining a reporter for conducting an interview — the only issue that interrogators questioned him about — is a violation of international law,” Lander said when he published the letter. “It comes at a time when senior Israeli officials are trying to delegitimize the participation of Palestinian citizens in Israel’s recent elections.”

Nor do Israel’s problems end with angry Democrats. The wounded Republican establishment lost no time looking a few thousand miles away to find reasons for the collapse of its voter base.

Soon after the election results came in, the vice-president, JD Vance, put “our relationship with Israel” on a short list of reasons for voter fury, and on election day Trump made a last-ditch attempt to woo voters with a pledge to cut off $4bn (£3bn) in annual military aid to Israel.

The announcement caused panic in Israel’s defence establishment. “When the commander of the Israel air force hears something like that, he might slit his wrists,” one official told Channel 12 news. “Where are we going to come up with 15 billion shekels every year, and what does that mean for Israel’s future defence budget?”

Netanyahu only responded to Trump’s electioneering on Friday with an attempt to spin the cut as a joint decision reflecting Israel’s economic strength. It demonstrated a “move from aid to partnership”, his office said in a statement.

Netanyahu has long flaunted his relationship with Trump, his fluent English and experience in the US, presenting himself as the only man with the international standing to guarantee Israel’s security in a hostile world.

After Tuesday’s US election, he looks more like an agent of its destruction to many in Israel. “One thing is clear: we are losing America,” Ben Caspit wrote in Ma’ariv, a daily newspaper.

“This isn’t a process; it isn’t happening in stages; it is happening all at once. It is an avalanche. It is a reverberating collapse of the foundation of Israel’s national defence doctrine. This isn’t a decree of fate. It is a decree of Netanyahu.”

Some advocates for change inside Israel found cause for hope in the Democrats’ victory, if Israel’s opposition can turn their mandate for change into a new government. They won 67 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, but more than a quarter went to Palestinian citizens of Israel, and some of the Jewish Israeli opposition parties have ruled out sitting with them.

US administrations have for too long equated support for Israel with blind support for its government, said Nadav Tamir, a former senior Israeli diplomat in the US who is now executive director of J Street Israel.

That consensus is cracking, but the majority of lawmakers from both parties still see Israel as a key US ally in the Middle East, he wrote in the Times of Israel.

External pressure from those who support its security but see current policy as self-destructive might push the country towards necessary change, including a resolution of the Israel-Palestine conflict.

“Perhaps this will be the paradox of the new [US] Congress,” he wrote. “It will be less willing to define support for Israel as automatic alignment with every policy of its government, but precisely for that reason, it may offer Israel more meaningful support in breaking out of the cycle of wars and building a future of security and prosperity.”

articles.title: In Sudafrica l’Anc non fa più presa nelle città
articles.summary: I sudafricani hanno votato per le amministrative con in mente i problemi causati dalla cattiva gestione dei servizi pubblici. Per l’African national congress il verdetto è stato duro
articles.preview: Il 4 novembre, mentre il resto del mondo era concentrato sui risultati delle elezioni di metà mandato negli Stati Uniti, i sudafricani sono andati alle urne per rinnovare più di 10.500 consigli municipali, tra cui quelli delle otto città metropolitane, che comprendono centri importanti come Pretoria, Johannesburg, Città del Capo, Durban e Bloemfontein. La legge sudafricana non prevede l’elezione diretta del sindaco, che viene scelto dal nuovo consiglio locale entro 14 giorni dal voto.
articles.body:
Il 4 novembre, mentre il resto del mondo era concentrato sui risultati delle elezioni di metà mandato negli Stati Uniti, i sudafricani sono andati alle urne per rinnovare più di 10.500 consigli municipali, tra cui quelli delle otto città metropolitane, che comprendono centri importanti come Pretoria, Johannesburg, Città del Capo, Durban e Bloemfontein.

La legge sudafricana non prevede l’elezione diretta del sindaco, che viene scelto dal nuovo consiglio locale entro 14 giorni dal voto. Quindi le preferenze di elettori ed elettrici – la cui affluenza alle urne è stata del al 54,5 per cento, in crescita rispetto al 2021 – non si rivolgono a singoli candidati, ma hanno anche un importante valore di termometro politico, in particolare sull’operato dell’African national congress (Anc), il partito nato dal movimento di liberazione guidato da Nelson Mandela, che è al potere dalla fine dell’apartheid, nel 1994.

Come previsto prima del voto, il verdetto è stato spietato. Già dai risultati parziali delle elezioni amministrative è apparso chiaramente che il partito del presidente Cyril Ramaphosa ha perso gran parte di quel consenso e di quella legittimità che gli avevano permesso di governare indisturbato per trent’anni. E li ha persi a causa dei pessimi servizi pubblici erogati alla popolazione, a cominciare dalla distribuzione dell’acqua potabile.

Un’immagine del vignettista Zapiro riassume bene la situazione: dalla torre per le telecomunicazioni, simbolo di Johannesburg, sporge un rubinetto – gestito dall’Anc – da cui esce un’unica goccia d’acqua, che cade nel secchio vuoto dei voti per il partito. Sullo sfondo, alcune persone fanno la fila per prendere l’acqua da un camion cisterna. “È a secco!”, commenta un funzionario vestito con i colori del partito. “Chissà come mai…”, risponde una signora.

Uno dei temi principali della campagna elettorale è stato proprio l’accesso all’acqua potabile, uno dei problemi più gravi per le popolazioni urbane del Sudafrica, in un contesto generale di dissesto finanziario, infrastrutture carenti o in stato di abbandono, interruzioni di corrente elettrica e cattiva gestione della raccolta dei rifiuti.

Secondo il sito sudafricano Groundup, in più della metà delle città che si occupano del trattamento dell’acqua la qualità di quest’ultima è insoddisfacente, se non pessima. E, anche se la qualità dell’acqua è buona, le amministrazioni locali non sono sempre in grado di distribuirla efficacemente, a causa delle perdite nella rete idrica. Il risultato è che in alcune aree i residenti restano senz’acqua corrente per giorni. Secondo Groundup la situazione di oggi è leggermente migliore rispetto ai tempi della presidenza di Jacob Zuma (2009-2018), nota come il “decennio perduto” a causa dei livelli altissimi di corruzione e di appropriazione indebita delle risorse pubbliche. Ma c’è ancora molto lavoro da fare.

L’Anc ne ha pagato il conto. Il declino non è recente, come mostra questa mappa: se nel 2004 aveva ottenuto quasi il 70 per cento dei voti a livello nazionale, alle amministrative del 2021 il partito era sceso per la prima volta sotto il 50 per cento. Alle politiche del 2024 aveva registrato poco più del 40 per cento dei voti a suo favore ed era stato costretto per la prima volta a formare un governo di unità nazionale con altri nove partiti, tra cui la Democratic alliance (Da), il partito di riferimento della minoranza bianca. Dal suo feudo di Città del Capo, la Da, guidata da Helen Zille, 75 anni, ha cominciato a fare presa anche nel resto del paese, tanto che oggi rischia di strappare all’Anc il controllo di Pretoria e di Johannesburg, il motore economico del paese.

Zille, che in passato è stata criticata per le sue posizioni sulla questione razziale, si è proposta come candidata sindaca di Joburg, scommettendo sul fatto che i cittadini siano più interessati a temi come la qualità della vita e dei servizi, che alla sua appartenenza razziale. E il voto potrebbe non darle torto. Con queste elezioni l’Anc è diventato un “partito di campagna”, scrive il commentatore del Financial Times David Pilling.

La formazione è ancora radicata nelle zone rurali, ma è in caduta libera nelle grandi città, dove si fanno sentire di più i disservizi e gli altri problemi che affliggono il paese, come l’insicurezza dovuta alla criminalità e alla violenza politica (solo all’avvicinarsi di queste elezioni sono stati registrati venti casi di omicidi a sfondo politico). Se a livello nazionale i risultati preliminari danno l’Anc al 32 per cento, con la Da al 24 per cento, in città come Johannesburg e Pretoria il partito di Zille è decisamente in testa. A Durban, il più grande porto del paese, invece è andato forte il partito uMkhonto we Sizwe (Mk), dell’ex presidente Zuma, la Da è seconda e l’Anc terzo.

Si aprirà presto una fase di intense trattative per formare coalizioni stabili in grado di governare le grandi città del paese. L’Anc e la Da sono già partner nel governo nazionale dal 2024, e finora la loro alleanza ha resistito nonostante le molte divergenze. “Molti elettori sudafricani stanno cominciando a non votare più in base a criteri razziali ed etnici… per scegliere in base alla competenza” dei candidati, nota il commentatore sudafricano William Gumede sul Mail & Guardian. La speranza è che i vincitori di queste elezioni amministrative si dimostrino all’altezza.

Questo testo è tratto dalla newsletter Africana.

articles.title: What’s the point? Ten years after the Paris treaty, are climate talks getting anywhere?
articles.summary: Its key temperature goal has been missed but experts say the agreement is still proving a vital moral compass for progress It was a curious way of conducting negotiations. articles.preview: Its key temperature goal has been missed but experts say the agreement is still proving a vital moral compass for progress It was a curious way of conducting negotiations. Ahead of the 2025 climate summit, in the Amazonian port of Belém last year, the Brazilian hosts had taken off the table the issue that most had assumed would be at its heart: concrete plans from each country laying out exactly what they would be doing to cut their greenhouse gas emissions.
articles.body:
It was a curious way of conducting negotiations. Ahead of the 2025 climate summit, in the Amazonian port of Belém last year, the Brazilian hosts had taken off the table the issue that most had assumed would be at its heart: concrete plans from each country laying out exactly what they would be doing to cut their greenhouse gas emissions.

Brazil was insisting, instead, that these plans – the bedrock of the Paris agreement – were the business of national governments and not up for negotiation. “In that case, it will be a very short Cop,” one seasoned global south negotiator told the Guardian shortly before, reflecting a widespread unease. “There is nothing to negotiate.”

“They have decided that there is no appetite for negotiation, with the US out of Paris,” said another developing country diplomat. “Countries won’t engage.”

The summit ended with a deal, although few loved it. But, as the faultlines from the Brazilian decision deepen going into this year’s summit, it is clear that the Paris agreement, and climate action around the world, has reached an impasse.

And it is not just Cop insiders who are worried. For many outside the vast white air-conditioned conference halls, the question, as this year’s summit begins, will be: what is the point?

Those same governments have pledged year after year since the Paris agreement was signed in 2015 – and entered into force a year later – to limit global heating to 1.5C above preindustrial levels. Yet temperatures for two years have exceeded that threshold, and the UN revealed a few weeks ago that its most optimistic estimate was now for about 1.7 to 1.8C of heating.

There could be no clearer evidence that the Paris agreement, on the face of it, has failed. It is impossible not to wonder whether the Cop process itself is just not fit for purpose.

The charge sheet against Paris is long, with the central issue being the failure to achieve its goal. Beyond that immediate failure, the negotiation processes are endlessly convoluted and cause their own problems. It took more than five years just to negotiate the Paris “rulebook” under which the treaty is interpreted and put into effect.

The convention that all resolutions must pass by consensus has given bad actors free rein. Donald Trump’s allies – in Saudi Arabia, Russia, Venezuela and some other petrostates – frequently veto measures and obstruct progress.

It took more than 30 years of negotiation since the UN framework convention on climate change was signed in 1992 for fossil fuels even to be addressed directly. This was at Cop28 in Dubai in 2023, where countries agreed for the first time to “transition away from fossil fuels” but failed to set a timeframe or any policies to back up the resolution.

The US, the world’s biggest economy and responsible for about one in every eight tonnes of carbon dioxide emitted today, has withdrawn from Paris under President Trump.

Even parts of the developed world which support the process have mostly failed to come up with convincing plans: Australia, co-host of Cop31, has set no end to fossil fuel exports; its fellow co-host Turkey plans to increase its carbon output. The UK is opening a gasfield and mulling a new oilfield, Germany has dropped its electric vehicle sales targets and scrapped a renewable heating law. Meanwhile, most rich countries are reducing their contributions to climate finance for the poor.

Most of all, the slow pace of the Paris timetable might have seemed fine in 2015, when temperatures were rising at 0.2C a decade. Today, the rate of rise is 0.4C a decade and still accelerating.

“The structures of Cops and Paris are labyrinthine, bureaucratic, and ultimately dispiriting,” said Paul Bledsoe, a former Clinton White House climate adviser, now with the American University. “It may be time to streamline them to focus more deliberately on national emissions reduction goals.”

As ordinary people watch these failures outside and inside the process, some are losing faith. The Paris agreement was a sensation, celebrated around the world. In the years since, the aura of Cop has faded, as meetings seem to disintegrate into arguments over wording and compromise.

“A lot of the commitments, the promises that were made, just turned out to be a bunch of hot air,” said Juan Carlos Monterrey, former climate envoy for Panama, now chief executive of the Vanglabs consultancy. “Under that measure, we have failed.”

Johan Rockström, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, said: “The fact that global warming is accelerating, that we inevitably will be breaching the 1.5C limit within three to five years, that tipping points are coming closer fast, that Earth’s resilience is showing worrying signs of decline, and that we still allow ourselves to follow a global path that will take us to a catastrophic 2.6C-3C, and that this is allowed to happen within the framework of the Paris agreement, cannot be considered as anything but a global failure.”

But, like most involved in international climate efforts, both refuse to concede that Paris is done for. “On the other hand,” said Rockström, “Paris is all we have. And we know that the global climate crisis can only, in the end, be solved if all countries in the world simultaneously move away from planet-damaging heat injection.”

Monterrey agrees. The most important fact about the Paris agreement, and the Cop process, he says, is that they exist. “Paris is our moral compass. It has told us where we should go. The speed of travel is not what it needs to be, but Paris has set the direction.”

A messy compromise

This year’s Cop is the first to have a split presidency and host. Being held in Turkey but presided over by Australia, Cop31 is a messy compromise between two countries whose other chief point of commonality is an admiration for coal.

Unexpectedly, however, the skies are a little brighter over this year’s meeting than anyone might have expected. Brazil has decisively re-elected Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva who has already overseen the biggest reductions in deforestation for decades.

The US midterms delivered a drubbing for the right, while in Serbia and Hungary this year democracy has won out over authoritarianism. Though the far right is still on the march across much of Europe, and autocrats still rule in most of the countries with the biggest fossil fuel industries and highest emissions, the replacement or weakening of anti-climate authoritarians by pro-climate parties is a positive sign. Globally, a large majority of people support climate action.

Action beyond the framework of Cop is marching on. After the failure of last year’s Cop30 in Brazil to provide a strong statement on phasing out fossil fuels, a group of nearly 60 countries held an alternative meeting in Colombia in April and agreed to draw up their own national roadmaps for the “transition away from fossil fuels”.

Three major countries have so far done so: France, Germany and the Netherlands. Bledsoe wants to use this model for more side agreements on the “super pollutants” such as methane, refrigerant chemicals called HFCs, ground-level ozone, nitrous oxide and black carbon, or soot.

Cutting methane by 40% could alone hold down temperatures by about 0.3C in the next decade, and deeper cuts beyond that could yield a 0.5C decrease by 2100.

“Paris was never intended to do all the hard work itself,” Bledsoe said. “We need to use the G7, the G20 and other forums too, and we need to elevate the climate to the level of national security concern, and see it as an economic threat.”

While the failures of Paris might seem obvious, its “moral compass” has also translated into greater success in the real world than many people realise.

“The solar panels on my roof and the BYD Dolphin [electric car] my neighbour drives are exhibit one and exhibit two of Paris’s success,” said Claudio Angelo, of the Observatório do Clima thinktank. “Will Paris prevent overshoot of 1.5C? No way. Will it prevent 2C of warming? Unlikely. But the transformation it has triggered can’t be exaggerated.”

Perhaps the clinching argument lies in China, the world’s biggest emitter of greenhouse gases and second-largest economy.

“China is taking multilateral climate efforts more seriously than many other countries, and certainly more seriously than it did a few years ago,” said Li Shuo, director of the China climate hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute. “The reason is simple: its economic stakes have grown enormously. If the world abandons decarbonisation, where will China sell its solar panels and electric vehicles?”

And, stung by high fossil fuel prices, many developing-country consumers are grasping clean technology without waiting for assistance. In Pakistan, plagued by blackouts and grid supply issues, rooftop solar panels have taken off, now making up about a quarter of electricity use in the country. Similarly, drivers in Vietnam are increasingly opting for cheap electric vehicles from China, which now make up more than 40% of its car sales.

Meanwhile, the conference hosts themselves, from unpromising beginnings, have brought forward one of the biggest new ideas in the last decade for putting the world on track to lower emissions – changing fuel sources for cars and heating to electricity. The electricity should be from clean sources where possible – but its efficiency means that even if the energy source is fossil-based, it still uses less power.

Jan Rosenow, professor of energy and climate policy at Oxford University, estimates that the superior efficiency of electricity over fossil fuels will mean that the world’s total final energy use can be halved by switching to electric for everything – meaning we need to generate a lot less, too.

If countries can agree a target at Cop31 of deriving 35% of final energy use from electricity by 2035, up from 23% today, that would be a major boost to decarbonisation efforts. Adair Turner, former chair of the UK’s climate change committee and now co-chair of the Energy Transitions Commission thinktank, said: “Electrification is the single most important thing you have to do [to reach net zero emissions].”

Cops provide a place where countries can come together to share experiences, to seek advice, to find support and fellowship. “That’s very valuable,” said Ilana Seid, ambassador of Palau and chair of the Pacific Small Island Developing States. And in a world in which the bulk of current and future emissions, and fossil fuel production, comes from non-democracies or authoritarian states, Cops also provides one of the few forums where they can be held to account.

That “societal pressure” is crucial, said Seid. “We small islands and vulnerable nations are on the frontline. For us, this is existential. We are all very committed to Paris.”

After all, despite all the doubts, the power of a decision at Cop should not be underestimated. While “coalitions of the willing” are a “good thing” according to Nick Stern, the economist, the universality of the Paris agreement and Cops give them a unique authority.

Sue Biniaz, a former US climate negotiator, said: “Any time you have a consensus decision, it sends a signal to investors, to people who finance things, and to countries. I think that’s true these days with the geopolitics of the world – if something can be agreed by the whole world, it’s impactful.”

Cop31 may bring progress on electrification, on climate finance and on the transition that countries, rich and poor, need to make to a low-carbon world. But we already know that whatever the summit produces, it will not be enough.

However flawed yet substantive they are, Cops last only a fortnight, while efforts to tackle the climate crisis will require such wholesale transformation of our economies and societies that they should top governments’ agendas all year.

“Imagine you have lost your loved one without having their bodies to bring back home. Lost livelihood where you spent your whole life to accumulate those assets. We faced a horrific situation,” said Sujeeta Mathema, executive director of ActionAid Nepal, who was quickly on the scene to help people after the catastrophic glacier collapse there.

“It feels like living with grief, fear and uncertainty about the future. The devastation is not just physical; it is deeply emotional and psychological.”

People are traumatised, she says, and deeply feel the injustice of how the climate crisis is created by the rich while hurting the most vulnerable. But Cop can still be a place of hope, Mathema adds.

“Cop is an important space for us to raise our voice, clearly putting our agenda. Cop can help prevent such disasters if the commitments come off paper and are put into action.”

articles.title: Cina, dalla bolla immobiliare alla bolla delle auto

articles.body:
A settembre le case automobilistiche cinesi hanno registrato una diminuzione dei profitti pari al 68 per cento rispetto allo stesso periodo di un anno fa. Il calo riguarda quasi tutti i maggiori produttori: nel terzo trimestre del 2026 la Saic Motor, la leader di mercato, ha registrato utili in discesa del 76,7 per cento; la Chongqing Changan Automobile ha perso 760 milioni di yuan (poco più di cento milioni di euro); la Anhui Jianghuai Automobile Group ha avuto una perdita netta di 1,1 miliardi di yuan nei primi nove mesi del 2026; la Seres Group ha registrato un utile netto di 1,4 miliardi di yuan nel terzo trimestre di quest’anno, ma se si escludono le voci non legate alla normale attività dell’azienda risulta una perdita di 1,4 miliardi di yuan. I rappresentanti del settore automobilistico cinese hanno dichiarato che il 2026 potrebbe chiudersi con 18,5 milioni di veicoli venduti, il dato peggiore dal 2014.

Le cause sono l’aumento dei costi e il crollo della domanda interna. Un fatto poco sorprendente in un paese dove la popolazione invecchia costantemente e in generale consuma poco (i consumi cinesi corrispondono al 40 per cento del pil, contro il 70 per cento degli Stati Uniti), i trasporti pubblici sono abbastanza efficienti e i taxi a guida autonoma sono ormai una realtà in molti centri urbani. Per questo sul più grande mercato automobilistico del mondo, spiega il sito Caixin Global, è in corso da tempo una brutale corsa al ribasso dei prezzi tra le numerosissime aziende del settore, una selezione darwiniana che sta mettendo in ginocchio molte di loro.

La posta in gioco

Il dato suscita non pochi interrogativi: com’è possibile che il settore sia in calo mentre il resto del mondo – l’Europa innanzitutto, basta pensare ai guai della Volkswagen – è letteralmente inondato dai veicoli cinesi? La risposta più immediata è che in Cina si è creata una bolla simile a quella che negli scorsi anni ha devastato il settore immobiliare: c’è un forte eccesso di produzione che finora è stato ampiamente assorbito attraverso le esportazioni; ma tutto questo potrebbe non bastare più. Com’è successo nel caso dell’immobiliare, inoltre, non sarà facile assorbire quest’altra bolla, soprattutto perché anche in questo caso, oltre ad aziende e posti di lavoro, è in gioco la stabilità di molti enti locali cinesi, profondamente coinvolti nello sviluppo del settore automobilistico.

Un interessante articolo del Wall Street Journal racconta il caso della Skyworth Auto, un’azienda che nel 2021 sosteneva di poter produrre centomila auto elettriche all’anno, ma che nei primi nove mesi del 2026 ha venduto appena 660 vetture. La Skyworth oggi resta in vita grazie agli aiuti del distretto di Nanchino, che possiede il 5 per cento del suo capitale. Un anno fa, scrive il quotidiano statunitense, sul sito web dell’amministrazione di Nanchino si leggeva che la Skyworth aveva ricevuto “il sostegno completo di tutti i dipartimenti governativi” e che l’aiuto dell’amministrazione aveva permesso di superare “gli ostacoli incontrati dall’azienda nel suo sviluppo”.

La Skyworth non è un’eccezione. Per anni gli enti locali cinesi hanno stretto alleanze con i privati per investire nel settore automobilistico: ogni città puntava sul “campione locale” sperando di diventare la Detroit cinese. Il fenomeno si è accentuato con l’arrivo dell’auto elettrica: alla fine del 2025 le aziende cinesi di auto elettriche che vendevano almeno un modello erano 143. La Nio, azienda pioniere del settore oggi quotata alla borsa di Wall street, stava per dichiarare insolvenza prima che nel 2020 l’amministrazione comunale di Hefei la salvasse con un investimento di quasi settecento milioni di dollari. La città voleva costruire intorno alla Nio un parco industriale dedicato alle auto elettriche con l’obiettivo di dare lavoro a migliaia di persone.

La proliferazione di accordi simili, unita al credito facile concesso dalle banche, ha fatto nascere un settore abnorme in grado di fabbricare 63 milioni di auto all’anno, più del triplo di quelle che nel 2026 dovrebbero essere comprate dai cinesi. Il resto finisce all’estero, su un mercato globale che ogni anno assorbe circa 85 milioni di auto (settanta se si escludono gli Stati Uniti, un mercato praticamente inaccessibile ai cinesi).

Di fronte al calo della domanda interna, alle aziende cinesi restano due scelte, aggiunge il Wall Street Journal: da un lato riducono i prezzi per accaparrarsi una fetta del mercato interno (dall’inizio del 2023 i prezzi dei veicoli cinesi sono diminuiti di quasi il 20 per cento); dall’altro puntano sulle esportazioni (quest’anno la Cina dovrebbe vendere all’estero dodici milioni di auto, all’inizio del decennio in corso le vendite annuali si aggiravano sul milione), sfruttando tra l’altro uno yuan perennemente svalutato da Pechino.

Ora la Cina comincia ad accorgersi che questa strategia non può continuare a lungo: all’interno i prezzi non possono scendere ulteriormente; all’estero gli altri paesi cominciano a reagire all’ondata di auto cinesi, che sta mettendo in ginocchio le loro aziende. Insomma, addossare al resto del mondo i punti deboli della propria economia non è la soluzione.

Il problema è che il presidente Xi Jinping non sembra avere il pieno controllo della situazione, soprattutto perché molte amministrazioni locali invischiate nel settore automobilistico non hanno intenzione di staccare la spina alle aziende, sia perché temono di perdere tanti posti di lavoro sia perché vedrebbero ridursi le loro entrate fiscali, danneggiando ulteriormente finanze già messe a dura prova dall’esplosione della bolla immobiliare.

La spirale del debito

La Cina, lanciata da Xi Jinping in grandiosi progetti legati alle tecnologie militari e civili più avanzate (dai pannelli solari all’intelligenza artificiale), è finita in una pericolosa spirale del debito: nel 2025 i prestiti concessi a settori non finanziari – grandi conglomerati industriali, enti pubblici e famiglie – hanno raggiunto il 300 per cento del pil nazionale, 60 punti percentuali in più rispetto alla fine del 2019 e 43mila miliardi di dollari in più del 2012, cioè da quando Xi è arrivato al potere. Molto di questo denaro è stato buttato prima in immobili che oggi non vuole nessuno e poi in fabbriche che perdono soldi perché non trovano abbastanza acquirenti e non possono più di tanto abbassare i prezzi o decurtare i salari degli operai.

L’enorme mole di debiti e attività in perdita forse non provocherà una crisi finanziaria in un paese come la Cina, ma di sicuro ne sta indebolendo l’economia. Le prospettive rosee suscitate dalla straordinaria crescita degli ultimi decenni stanno lasciando il posto al pessimismo: quello di molti giovani, che fanno fatica a trovare occupazioni adeguate alle loro competenze; e quello di molti lavoratori che, tagliati fuori dall’automazione, ormai si riciclano nel mondo precario della gig economy (quest’anno il numero dei cosiddetti gig worker cinesi dovrebbe arrivare a 320 milioni, contro i 280 milioni del 2025).

Xi forse pensa che tutto si possa risolvere quando la Cina si affermerà come una potenza globale del livello degli Stati Uniti, se non superiore a loro. Anche per questo continua a ignorare gli appelli di molti economisti – cinesi e non – che consigliano di far crescere i consumi interni: questa svolta darebbe respiro sia alle aziende in cerca di clienti sia ai lavoratori, oltre a creare nuove entrate per lo stato e le amministrazioni locali; ne sarebbero felici anche gli altri paesi, alle prese con l’ondata di esportazioni cinesi.

Tuttavia, aumentare i consumi interni ridurrebbe la presa di Pechino sull’economia nazionale e distoglierebbe capitali da settori che Xi giudica strategici. Intanto, per aiutare le finanze pubbliche Pechino ha lanciato una vasta campagna contro l’evasione e l’elusione fiscale dei ricchi cinesi. Ma come osservano gli economisti Navneeraj Sharma e Arvind Subramanian, a questo punto “è probabile che si verifichi un lento declino caratterizzato da una crescita anemica, un crescente malcontento e un deterioramento dei servizi”. Comunque sufficiente per avere ripercussioni sull’intera economia globale.

Questo testo è tratto dalla newsletter Economica.

Por su menguante tirón político, incluso entre los suyos: el batacazo en bastiones conservadores como Texas, Kansas o el sur profundo de Misisipi , ha sido de aúpa.
