articles.title: ‘They started bombing us with drones’: Russian attacks unnerve Zaporizhzhia
articles.summary: A region once offering refuge becomes increasingly dangerous, as 50 people are killed in a single attack.
articles.preview: A region once offering refuge becomes increasingly dangerous, as 50 people are killed in a single attack. Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine – There are only eight people left in Volodymyr’s village. That was the last count he remembers before deciding to leave. “We were in the cellar when they started bombing us with drones,” he said, nervously rubbing his red, blistered hands together.
articles.body:
A region once offering refuge becomes increasingly dangerous, as 50 people are killed in a single attack.

Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine – There are only eight people left in Volodymyr’s village. That was the last count he remembers before deciding to leave.

“We were in the cellar when they started bombing us with drones,” he said, nervously rubbing his red, blistered hands together. “As you can see, I was completely burned.”

Last week, he fled his home in Preobrazhenka, just over 40km (25 miles) from where he now sits in a shelter for displaced people in the regional capital, Zaporizhzhia.

The villages south of Zaporizhzhia have been coming under escalating Russian attacks.

On November 2, in one of this year’s deadliest attacks in Ukraine, nine Russian glide bombs struck the town of Komyshuvakha, killing at least 50 people. Many had gathered to receive humanitarian aid at a local school. Several people are still missing, feared dead under the rubble.

The constant threat of bombs and drones makes everyday life almost unbearable.

Over the past three years, this war has proven that an army no longer needs boots on the ground.

The arrival of Russian First-Person-View (FPV) drones overhead is often a sign of the Russian infantry’s gradual advance. Well-documented footage shows these drones deliberately targeting vehicles and civilians on the streets. Ukrainians say drones have stalked civilians in cities including Kherson, Kramatorsk and Sloviansk.

Now, Zaporizhzhia is showing some of the same warning signs.

The city administration is doing what it can to protect residents, installing anti-drone netting over streets and civilian infrastructure in the Cosmos neighbourhood. But boarded-up windows and bombed-out buildings across the city show how difficult it is to mitigate the threat once the drones arrive.

Denys Knysh, a regional military administration official, says authorities are preparing to relocate the shelter where Volodymyr is staying to another neighbourhood “if the situation gets worse”.

Many in the shelter are elderly or have limited mobility. Some lack the documents they need to relocate, making evacuation more difficult.

Others prefer to stay in Zaporizhzhia, close to their former homes, holding on to hope that the war will end and they can return.

Since the beginning of the war, Zaporizhzhia has provided refuge for thousands of internally displaced people fleeing Russia’s occupation. People have arrived from cities like Mariupol and Melitopol, which fell under Russian control early in the conflict.

Now, as the security situation deteriorates, some of those who once fled to Zaporizhzhia for safety face the prospect of having to leave again.

Alina, who works in a flower shop beneath protective drone netting, said, “Of course I may have to leave, but I don’t want to.”

She hears the buzz of Russian drones almost every day.

Nearby, along the Pryberezhna Highway that follows the river, every petrol station and business is covered in the protective netting.

“It’s scary and dangerous, everything is flying around. Just today a drone flew over us,” said Nataliia, an employee at a petrol station.

Earlier that day, Russian Banderol missiles, a type of low-cost, jet-powered cruise missile, struck a shopping mall and the main bridge into the city. An FPV drone also hit a city bus.

Zaporizhzhia still has signs of normality. Twinkling lights hang over restaurant terraces and some streets still buzz with life.

But the transition is rarely clear-cut.

People gradually adapt to each new threat. It starts with streets covered in nets. Then drone jammers on the roofs of city buses. Bridges bear gaping holes from attacks. Children walk around carrying drone detectors.

Knysh says authorities are ready to evacuate the city if and when that time comes.

“It’s very difficult to calculate [how many people are left in the city] because every day people leave Zaporizhzhia,” he told Al Jazeera. “The demographic in Google doesn’t correspond to the reality.”

articles.title: Buildings damaged in Israeli bombings risk collapse as rain inundates Gaza
articles.summary: Floods have swept through Gaza after heavy rain, endangering families and putting war-damaged buildings at risk.
articles.preview: Floods have swept through Gaza after heavy rain, endangering families and putting war-damaged buildings at risk. Gaza City – Rana Adnan Hmeida, 29, stands at the entrance to her tent in al-Mina camp in northern Gaza, holding her two-month-old daughter as she tries to keep her warm after rainwater has flooded their shelter overnight. The family’s bedding, blankets and clothes are all soaked, with her children exposed to the cold and wind of Gaza’s latest storm.
articles.body:
Floods have swept through Gaza after heavy rain, endangering families and putting war-damaged buildings at risk.

Gaza City – Rana Adnan Hmeida, 29, stands at the entrance to her tent in al-Mina camp in northern Gaza, holding her two-month-old daughter as she tries to keep her warm after rainwater has flooded their shelter overnight. The family’s bedding, blankets and clothes are all soaked, with her children exposed to the cold and wind of Gaza’s latest storm.

Hmeida, her husband and children have been awake since midnight as heavy rain and strong winds swept through the camp. Water seeped into the tent and drenched their belongings. With all their clothes wet, Hmeida had to ask neighbours to help dry their clothes.

“Since midnight, we have been sitting awake. Water came into our tent, and the bedding, blankets and everything else got soaked. In the morning, I found my son and little daughter shivering. My two-month-old baby was freezing,” Hmeida told Al Jazeera.

“What am I supposed to do? Hold my children or try to stop the water? I was trying to keep them warm while carrying my little girl, but the water kept coming in. The wind was so strong that we felt the tent was about to be ripped out of the ground.”

Her husband, Sameh Hmeida, 30, said the family’s tent is particularly exposed due to its close proximity to the sea. It has no tarpaulins or insulating materials that might have helped in the storm.

Heavy rain has flooded camps and cities across Gaza over the past days, where many Palestinians are spending the fourth winter outside their homes since Israel began its genocidal war on the enclave in October 2023.

Water levels have risen by 30 to 40cm (12 to 16in) at several camps in Gaza due to Saturday’s rain, with Gaza’s civil defence agency receiving hundreds of calls.

Rainwater has flooded many tents in al-Mina camp, where about 1,700 Palestinian families live, turning the ground into pools of muddy water.

Raed Abu Amsha, 40, said his tent collapsed on top of his family during the storm. The clothes and blankets of all nine children in his care, four of them from his late brother, were soaked.

“I am responsible for orphans as well as my own children, and I cannot provide for their needs. This storm lasted only two hours, and look what it did to us. We need tents, tarpaulins and anything that can protect our children. How long are we going to keep living like this?” he said.

In Nuseirat, a decades-old camp in central Gaza with permanent structures, rainfall also threatens families living in buildings damaged by Israeli bombardments.

Nasser al-Hajj, 54, lives in a tower block that was hit in an Israeli strike in September 2025. Debris from upper floors fell onto his home, leaving a large hole in the ceiling where water now enters every time it rains.

Although the ceiling has been reinforced with support beams, an engineer has warned al-Hajj that the apartment is dangerous, with the risk of further rubble falling from the building if more bad weather hits Gaza.

During the latest storm, al-Hajj took his children to a neighbour’s home and waited for the debris to stop falling from the roof. Two of his children, who have autism, sleep in the tower block’s guard room, away from the damaged area.

“I am forced to live somewhere that could collapse over our heads at any moment. But where am I supposed to go? Rent is expensive, and a tent is not safe either,” he told Al Jazeera. “I know how dangerous this place is, but I have no other option,” he added.

According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), about 950,000 displaced people in Gaza are living in areas exposed to flooding. Low-lying locations and sites near the coast are particularly vulnerable, with more than 400,000 people living in areas considered at high risk of flooding.

About 44,000 Palestinians are living in structurally unsafe buildings, while more than 4,000 buildings across the territory are estimated to require full or partial demolition due to damage caused by Israeli air strikes. About 294,250 families need shelter assistance ahead of winter, but the available supplies cover only 18 percent of their needs.

The Gaza Municipality is also struggling to respond to the storms. About 15 kilometres of rainwater drainage lines and 212 kilometres of sewage networks have been damaged. Eight pumping stations and three main stormwater collection basins are out of service.

The remaining system can handle no more than 20 percent of rainwater under the best of circumstances, according to municipality spokesperson Hosni Muhanna.

“[We] continue to clean drainage systems in preparation for the rainy season,” Muhanna said.

The municipality has deployed workers to clean drains and manholes, remove rubbish and clear water channels, repair damaged sections of drainage lines and operate water pumps.

But Muhanna warns that these efforts cannot restore the network’s capacity amid shortages of fuel, equipment and spare parts.

More than 2,000 buildings in Gaza City alone are at risk of collapse, he said, and the volume of rubble in Gaza City has exceeded 25 million tonnes.

Emergency committees in displacement camps are also struggling with shortages of shelter supplies. Adli Awad, an official with the emergency committee in Nuseirat refugee camp, said his team is trying to distribute tents and tarpaulins, particularly to families affected by the rain. But the number of people in need far exceeds available stocks.

“We are trying to provide as many tents and tarpaulins as possible. We are also helping families dig channels to divert rainwater away from tents and reduce flooding,” Awad said.

articles.title: Blackouts and water shortages in Kyiv after Russia strikes Ukraine’s energy grid
articles.summary: Moscow used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in attacks on electricity substations and bridge over the Dnipro Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of trying to “plunge Kyiv and the entire country into a blackout”, after a major attack overnight on energy infrastructure in the capital and a bridge over the Dnipro River. Ukraine’s president said Moscow’s preparations for peace talks next week involved pummelling a city of millions with ballistic missiles. Continue reading...

Ukraine’s president said Moscow’s preparations for peace talks next week involved pummelling a city of millions with ballistic missiles. Continue reading...
articles.body:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of trying to “plunge Kyiv and the entire country into a blackout”, after a major attack overnight on energy infrastructure in the capital and a bridge over the Dnipro River.

Ukraine’s president said Moscow’s preparations for peace talks next week involved pummelling a city of millions with ballistic missiles.

Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the US are due to meet on Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war.

Zelenskyy appealed to the US Congress – won by the Democrats in the midterm elections – to pay more attention to Ukraine in the face of relentless Russian bombardment. “Ukraine must not be left alone. We are counting on increased bilateral support from the US,” he said.

Russia used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in its latest attack on Kyiv and surrounding regions. The city faced serious difficulties with its electricity, water and heat supplies, Zelenskyy said, with five people injured including a 14-year-old girl.

The strikes targeted substations in five regions, including one connecting two nuclear power plants to Kyiv. The city’s Northern Bridge, a key transport artery, was closed on Saturday as workers repaired damage to the road’s surface and power lines.

The attacks cap a dire week for residents in Kyiv, who have experienced day-long power cuts and interruptions to the water supply. Ukrainian officials say the Kremlin’s goal is to freeze civilians into submission over the brutal winter months, a war crime.

They have little confidence that US-backed peace talks will yield concrete results. In an interview with CNN, Zelenskyy described the latest blueprint set out by Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law, as “Yalta 2.0” – a reference to the 1945 summit between Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill that divided postwar Europe.

In a series of social media posts, Kushner said the discussions would include a new security framework for Europe, alongside guarantees for Ukraine. This appears to be a reference to the Kremlin’s longstanding demand that Nato’s expansion across Europe be reversed.

Speaking on Friday, Trump said a “big beautiful agreement” could be close, involving “all of Europe”. Shortly before invading Ukraine, the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, demanded that Nato go back to its pre-1997 posture – before the Baltic states and nations in eastern Europe and the Balkans joined.

Ukraine and its European partners are deeply sceptical. “The idea of discussing European-Russian security infrastructure is not simple, and it can be dangerous,” Zelenskyy told CNN, emphasising: “We don’t want to be divided by Russia.”

Zelenskyy said Moscow had to end its war first, with Ukraine given meaningful security guarantees. After that, “depending on the answers”, wider security architecture could be considered, he said. Western diplomats say agreeing to Russia’s demands would effectively end Nato.

Russia’s defence ministry, meanwhile, said its strikes early on Saturday were against energy and transport targets. Since the summer, it has dramatically stepped up air attacks on Ukrainian cities, as its progress on the frontline has stalled. Last month Russia lost 54,000 troops, killed or injured, according to Kyiv – the highest monthly loss in the war.

articles.title: Ukraine's power network suffers further damage after fresh Russian strikes
articles.summary: The attacks come before Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due to take part in trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next week.
articles.preview: Overnight drone and ballistic missile attacks damaged Ukrainian energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyhas said, causing blackouts and disrupting water supplies. Zelensky said 12 Ukrainian regions came under attack with the capital Kyiv hit hardest. Nine people are reported to have been hurt across the country, including one child, in the wave of attacks that consisted of more than 30 ballistic missiles and over 170 drones.
articles.body:
Overnight drone and ballistic missile attacks damaged Ukrainian energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyhas said, causing blackouts and disrupting water supplies.

Zelensky said 12 Ukrainian regions came under attack with the capital Kyiv hit hardest.

Nine people are reported to have been hurt across the country, including one child, in the wave of attacks that consisted of more than 30 ballistic missiles and over 170 drones.

The attacks come before Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due to take part in trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next week.

Zelensky wrote on Telegram, external that Moscow was preparing for the talks by launching attacks on Ukraine's "critical infrastructure".

Temperatures are dropping in Ukraine, and parts of the country have had the first winter snow.

"The situation in the capital is difficult, with disruptions to electricity, water, and heating supplies. Residential buildings, the North Bridge, and a kindergarten have been damaged," Zelensky said.

"In the Kyiv region, there were strikes on substations that connect the Rivne and Khmelnytsky nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central Ukraine."

In his latest update, Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the city's water supply system is back to operating normally. He also said around 60% of the city's apartment buildings were connected to the heating system.

The energy minister, Denys Shmyhal, said there were power cuts in five regions but did not say how many homes were affected.

Zelensky added that beyond Kyiv, substations were damaged in Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Kharkiv and Dnipro regions.

The latest attacks come after US First Lady Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House on Thursday.

She called for a "more enduring" ceasefire in Ukraine following a truce last week in the southern region of Kherson.

She thanked both Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin, making no reference to the origins of the war, which began when Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, which has caused thousands of civilian casualties and the displacement of millions.

Hundreds of residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky facing starvation and constant bombardment were able to evacuate during a six-day ceasefire, which both Moscow and Kyiv credited Trump with brokering.

"The lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace," she said.

Earlier this week, a number of people were killed when glide bombs hit an aid centre near Zaporizhzhia, with the death toll rising to 55 as teams search deeper into the ruins.

Zelensky added in his Telegram post on Saturday following the latest attacks that Ukraine was counting on increased bilateral support from the United States.

He wrote: "We are counting on unity between both parties on issues of security, support for Ukraine, condemnation of Russian aggression, and increased sanctions pressure on Putin.

"The resolve and consistency of the United States in supporting Ukraine are of great importance in bringing peace closer."

Meanwhile, Zelenksy's spokesperson would not be drawn on reports that the Ukrainian president is to be invited to the UK for a state visit next year.

articles.title: Centcom offers $20m reward for information about Iran's nuclear programme

articles.title: Qeshm island and Hormuz hit, as mediators try to prevent US-Iran escalation
articles.summary: US strikes have continued on Iran after more ships in the Strait of Hormuz were attacked.
articles.preview: US strikes have continued on Iran after more ships in the Strait of Hormuz were attacked. Tehran, Iran – The United States has bombed Iran after vessels were targeted in the Strait of Hormuz, as mediators continue to try to prevent large-scale fighting between the two countries. Two projectiles hit Iran’s Qeshm on Friday night, the latest in a series of air strikes on the southern island over recent weeks targeting Iranian air defences and launchers.
articles.body:
US strikes have continued on Iran after more ships in the Strait of Hormuz were attacked.

Tehran, Iran – The United States has bombed Iran after vessels were targeted in the Strait of Hormuz, as mediators continue to try to prevent large-scale fighting between the two countries.

Two projectiles hit Iran’s Qeshm on Friday night, the latest in a series of air strikes on the southern island over recent weeks targeting Iranian air defences and launchers. President Donald Trump called them “minor strikes”, amid increasing concerns of a potential escalation in the war between the countries.

Iran’s army said in the early hours of Saturday that it destroyed a US-made MQ-9 drone using an unnamed new system. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) separately claimed on Friday that its air defences intercepted an MQ-1, reportedly the 16th aircraft of this model to be destroyed since the start of the war.

At least 11 ships were attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz over the week ending on November 6, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), which said three of them sank. The Western military intelligence agency has recorded 88 projectile strikes since hostilities resumed in early July, although it has cautioned that most attacks are going unreported.

UKMTO’s weekly report also identified 170 outbound and 155 inbound transits in the Strait of Hormuz, approximately 65 percent below pre-conflict levels. Most of the vessels that travel with their transponders switched on are using the Iranian route to the north. But many ships are still attempting the southern route near Oman with their tracking systems offline to shuttle oil out of the waterway.

Iranian armed forces also claim that, in addition to being hit with missiles and drones, tankers and commercial vessels using “unauthorised” routes also run the risk of being hit by naval mines.

The Iranian military’s naval force said on Saturday that a tanker with its transponder turned off caught fire in the eastern area of the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a mine. Washington says the mines have been cleared.

No range limit on missiles

For years, the IRGC maintained that it was limiting the range of its ballistic missiles to about 2,000 kilometres (1,240 miles) to reassure European countries that they would not be targeted.

But with Trump threatening to resume extensive air strikes on Iran’s civilian infrastructure, commanders say nothing is off limits now.

“This limitation has been lifted for us,” IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi told reporters during an event on Saturday, in reference to missile range constraints.

His comments came after Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei ordered an unrestrained military response to any future threats from Israel and the US. Iran’s aerospace division of the IRGC has prepared “surprising defence achievements” that will be deployed in action if another wave of major attacks starts, he added.

“The operational unveiling of these [advanced] achievements in case of new conflict will not only frustrate and fascinate enemies, but will further solidify Iran’s military authority on the global stage, make the resistance front happy, and fully neutralise aggressors’ calculations,” Mohebbi said.

The spokesman said the IRGC plans to unveil another underground “missile city” soon, and will deploy some combat systems to public spaces so the people can personally inspect them.

Mohebbi added that if the Islamic republic decides to alter its nuclear doctrine and build a bomb, the necessary preparations will be made.

On state television’s war-focused Be Vaght-e Iran (At Iran’s Time) programme over the weekend, presenters and analysts said Iranian armed forces had their fingers on the trigger and were especially eyeing any movement from Israel.

“Our military information about the strategic chokepoints of Israel is complete. If our water, electricity and natural gas is cut off, they will also be plunged into darkness and lack of water,” one analyst said. “This is not a bluff, but a serious warning.”

‘Pendulum swing between war and talks’

Over recent weeks, diplomatic efforts by mediators to avoid attacks that could damage the entire region have picked up, although with limited gains.

Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Saturday that he held talks with 12 foreign ministers over the past 48 hours, including top diplomats from Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.

He said he explained the “fundamental positions” of Tehran, including the seven demands to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and stressed the need to form “regional security arrangements without the interference of superregional powers”.

Security chief Mohsen Rezaei reportedly emphasised the same conditions to Russian President Vladimir Putin during a visit to Moscow on Thursday, which was also aimed at delivering a message from Khamenei.

Developments between Iran and the US resemble a “constant pendulum swing between war and negotiations” that is increasingly leaning towards conflict, according to political analyst Mostafa Najafi, who is said to be close to Iran’s security chief.

“What is clear for now is that the movement of this pendulum will continue; a conflict whose ending is much more complicated and time-consuming than imagined,” he wrote on X. The historic defeat for Trump and the Republicans in US midterm elections this week may further complicate the picture, he added.

Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, said three factors increase the risk of war in the short term after the elections, unless negotiations lead to a breakthrough.

The political cost of high fuel prices, brought about largely due to the war on Iran, has already been paid, he said, and there won’t be another point on the political calendar soon for Trump to worry about this issue.

“On the one hand, the pressure to get a deal will dissipate,” he told Al Jazeera.

Pressure from pro-war hawks will also escalate significantly because they will be constrained in their efforts to step up the conflict after the Democrats take control of Congress in early January. The appointment of far-right, pro-Israel hawk Stephen Miller as chief of staff also hints that Trump might not be ready to wind down the war.

“Finally, there is a new psychological element to Trump’s mindset following this humiliation: Trump’s desire for vengeance. There has been a vindictive element to his calculations in the past weeks because of his anger over how Iran – in Trump’s mind – has ruined his presidency,” Parsi said.

articles.title: Nuovo attacco missilistico su Kiev. 'Situazione energetica estremamente difficile'
articles.summary: Colpite infrastrutture della capitale. Attacco ucraino con droni in diverse regioni russe
articles.preview: Nella notte tra il 6 e il 7 novembre, diverse ondate di missili balistici russi hanno colpito Kiev, poche ore dopo che il presidente Volodymyr Zelensky aveva avvertito che la Russia si stava preparando a un altro attacco su larga scala contro le infrastrutture. Lo riferisce The Kyiv Independent. Almeno cinque persone sono rimaste ferite nella capitale, tra cui una ragazza di 14 anni, secondo quanto riferito dal sindaco Vitali Klitschko.
articles.body:
Nella notte tra il 6 e il 7 novembre, diverse ondate di missili balistici russi hanno colpito Kiev, poche ore dopo che il presidente Volodymyr Zelensky aveva avvertito che la Russia si stava preparando a un altro attacco su larga scala contro le infrastrutture. Lo riferisce The Kyiv Independent.

Almeno cinque persone sono rimaste ferite nella capitale, tra cui una ragazza di 14 anni, secondo quanto riferito dal sindaco Vitali Klitschko. Il Ponte Nord di Kiev è stato danneggiato nell'attacco russo ed è stato chiuso al traffico in entrambe le direzioni, ha aggiunto Klitschko. Gli attacchi russi hanno danneggiato impianti energetici nella regione di Kiev, oltre a un ponte fondamentale nella capitale ucraina. Lo ha confermato il sindaco della città.

"A seguito di un attacco nemico avvenuto durante la notte, sono stati danneggiati impianti energetici nelle regioni di Kiev e di Žytomyr. La situazione relativa all'approvvigionamento energetico della capitale è estremamente difficile", ha scritto su Telegram il sindaco Vitali Klitschko. "Anche il Ponte del Nord è stato danneggiato in un attacco nemico. Gli specialisti stanno valutando l'entità dei danni", ha aggiunto Klitschko in un altro messaggio su Telegram.

L'Ucraina ha intanto colpito nella stessa notte diversi siti nelle regioni russe di Oryol, Saratov e Rostov, tra cui una raffineria di petrolio. Lo riferisce The Kyiv Independent. Secondo quanto riportato dal canale di monitoraggio Exilenova Plus, nella raffineria di petrolio di Saratov è scoppiato un incendio dopo un attacco ucraino con droni.

Secondo il governatore Roman Busargin, sono diverse le persone ferite. Un vasto incendio è scoppiato anche nei pressi della fabbrica militare Almaz nella città di Rostov, nel sud della Russia. Le fiamme sono state domate. Segnalate esplosioni anche nella città di Belgorod, dove, secondo quanto riferisce l'agenzia russa Ria Novosti, almeno una persona è rimasta ferita.

Zelensky:'Mosca si prepara ai colloqui trilaterali lanciandoci missili balistici'

"La Russia si prepara ai colloqui trilaterali lanciando missili balistici contro le infrastrutture critiche dell'Ucraina. Le operazioni di riparazione e soccorso sono attive nelle regioni colpite, ovunque la situazione della sicurezza lo consenta. In totale, i russi hanno utilizzato 172 droni e 36 missili balistici, tutti diretti contro Kiev e la regione circostante": lo ha affermato su X il leader ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky.

"Le infrastrutture energetiche sono state ancora una volta il principale obiettivo - ha proseguito il presidente ucraino - La capitale sta affrontando gravi difficoltà nell'approvvigionamento di elettricità, acqua e riscaldamento. Sono stati danneggiati edifici residenziali e il Ponte Nord. Un asilo è stato parzialmente distrutto". Zelensky ha aggiunto che, oltre a quella di Kiev, sono state colpite negli ultimi attacchi altre 12 regioni, e in tutto sono rimaste ferite nove persone, tra cui un bambino.

"Mentre la Russia cerca di gettare nell'oscurità Kiev, una città di milioni di abitanti, e l'intero Paese, l'Ucraina non deve essere lasciata sola. Contiamo su un maggiore sostegno bilaterale da parte degli Stati Uniti", è il suo appello.

articles.title: Yemeni government forces claim attack on Houthi positions in al-Misrakh, while Saudi attacks on Bani Hashih kill at least 15
articles.summary: Yemeni government forces claim attack on Houthi positions in al-Misrakh, while Saudi attacks on Bani Hashih kill at least 15 Yemeni government forces have claimed three air attacks on Houthi positions in the al-Misrakh district of the Taiz governorate. The city of Taiz- which is government-held- has been subject to an ongoing Houthi siege. The blockade has triggered a spiralling humanitarian crisis in the city, as road closures bar vital supplies, including fuel, from entering. Laurent Bukera, the United Nations Humanitarian Coordinator for Yemen warned that the city's health system is "close to collapse", while the UN World Food Programme (WFP) said that the conflict has blocked lifesaving assistance from reaching 800,000 people, including 600,000 who depend on aid in the city. Meanwhile, Houthi media reports that at least 15 people have been killed, mostly women and children, in a series of Saudi strikes in the al-Shariyah area of Yemen’s Bani Hashish district. According to the reports, some 30 others have been wounded.

articles.title: Trump afronta los dos últimos años de mandato como un octogenario desafiante obsesionado con las obras
articles.summary: Sin posibilidad de volver a presentarse y con un Congreso hostil, el republicano amenaza con plantar batalla y convertir el final de su presidencia en una guerra política con el nombramiento de Stephen Miller
articles.preview: Sin posibilidad de volver a presentarse y con un Congreso hostil, el republicano amenaza con plantar batalla y convertir el final de su presidencia en una guerra política con el nombramiento de Stephen Miller Al día siguiente de recibir un histórico revolcón electoral, Donald Trump solo parecía interesado en presumir de las obras del monumental salón de baile que está construyendo en el ala este de la Casa Blanca.
articles.body:
Sin posibilidad de volver a presentarse y con un Congreso hostil, el republicano amenaza con plantar batalla y convertir el final de su presidencia en una guerra política con el nombramiento de Stephen Miller

Al día siguiente de recibir un histórico revolcón electoral, Donald Trump solo parecía interesado en presumir de las obras del monumental salón de baile que está construyendo en el ala este de la Casa Blanca. Allí, entre material de obra oculto por banderas estadounidenses, imprimió su firma en la última viga de acero de la estructura, junto a dos pequeños sellos dorados que recuerdan su presidencia.

Durante la visita trató de eludir las preguntas sobre el resultado de las elecciones de medio mandato, en las que los demócratas le han arrebatado el control del Congreso en el mayor giro político desde los años del Watergate. La escena simboliza la actitud de un presidente desgastado que ha perdido abrumadoramente las últimas elecciones de su carrera: convertido de la noche a la mañana en un octogenario ensimismado en las obras que ha emprendido por todo Washington, obsesionado con dejar su legado en la arquitectura de la capital y eludiendo cualquier responsabilidad por el fracaso electoral.

Sin embargo, cuando todo el mundo en Washington debatía sobre el extraño comportamiento de Trump tras las elecciones —aceptó el resultado de primeras, cuando había dudas de que lo hiciera, y se mostró dispuesto a colaborar con los demócratas—, este viernes protagonizó su enésima jugada de prestidigitador. Nombró a Stephen Miller, uno de los hombres más radicales de su entorno, como nuevo jefe de Gabinete de la Casa Blanca, en sustitución de Susie Wiles, considerada la más moderada dentro del grupo de confianza del presidente.

La salida de Wiles se interpreta como un ajuste de cuentas tras la debacle electoral. Y el nombramiento de Miller, arquitecto de la política migratoria de la Casa Blanca con campañas de redadas y deportaciones masivas, plantea nuevas incógnitas sobre la actitud del republicano en el último tramo de su mandato justo cuando parecía que el trumpismo se desinflaba. ¿Mantendrá esa imagen de hombre obsesionado con su legado o querrá ir a la guerra política para impulsar su agenda conservadora? Esa es la gran pregunta ahora.

El ascenso de Miller revela otra característica de la personalidad de Trump: su carácter volcánico y vengativo. Aunque en los primeros compases parecía ajeno a la derrota en las midterms, el presidente estadounidense se fue enfadando conforme veía la cadena conservadora Fox News y leía los informes de prensa sobre la cobertura de la histórica derrota. La furia y la indignación se han ido extendiendo por la Casa Blanca a medida que transcurrían los días, buscando culpables del fracaso, según ha descrito la CNN.

El ascenso de Stephen Miller

El nombramiento de Miller, de 41 años, es toda una declaración de intenciones. Es un nacionalista radical, de ideas xenófobas y defensor de algunas de las políticas más polarizadoras de la Casa Blanca. Durante semanas dejó saber que quería el puesto de Wiles si esta renunciaba por sus problemas de salud (superó un cáncer hace unos meses), cansada de las intrigas internas y desesperada en sus intentos de frenar las iniciativas radicales de Miller y otros miembros del Gabinete, lo que le hizo perder la confianza del presidente.

Miller, sin embargo, es conocido por su extremismo, con discursos que algunos comparan con la retórica fascista de los años treinta del siglo pasado. Entre ellos, el que pronunció durante el funeral de Charlie Kirk, activista de derechas asesinado hace un par de años: “Nuestros enemigos no pueden comprender nuestra fuerza, nuestra determinación, nuestra resolución y nuestra pasión. No tenéis ni idea del dragón que habéis despertado”, dijo en referencia a sus adversarios políticos.

Al nombramiento de Miller se suma el mensaje que publicó Trump en redes sociales la noche electoral cuando difundió la imagen de una gorra roja con la palabra “VETO” en mayúsculas, en referencia al poder presidencial para bloquear las iniciativas del Congreso. Al día siguiente colocó la misma gorra sobre el histórico escritorio Resolute que preside el Despacho Oval.

Aunque ahora tiene menos poder, nadie cree que la era Trump haya concluido. “No debemos esperar que pase a un segundo plano. Y este no es (todavía) el final de su era”, advierte Lindsay Newman, investigadora del think tank Chatham House. “Como tantos otros aspectos de la política estadounidense en la última década, Trump está destinado a redefinir la presidencia saliente. Con las elecciones de mitad de mandato ya concluidas, el presidente puede ahora (re)centrarse en lo que más le importa: su legado”.

Un pato cojo “acorralado y enfadado”

Confirmado, además, como pato cojo, como se denomina a los presidentes que encaran los últimos años de su mandato, sin control sobre el Capitolio y con un partido, el republicano, en el que empiezan a aflorar las primeras fisuras del trumpismo, Trump afronta un difícil final de su mandato. Pero lo hace sin visos de que vaya a dejar a un lado su actitud retadora, pese a estar acorralado por unos índices de popularidad bajo mínimos y por un Congreso dominado por el Partido Demócrata decidido a condicionar su agenda, desmontar sus políticas más agresivas e investigar sus desmanes.

“Ahora que los demócratas controlan la Cámara de Representantes y el Senado, la amenaza de un juicio político o de investigaciones sobre los negocios de la familia Trump probablemente haría que el presidente se sintiera acorralado y enfadado”, advierte Daniel W. Drezner, en Foreign Affairs. “Y eso es lo que hace que el resto de su mandato sea tan peligroso. Un Trump acorralado, sin una vía clara para canalizar su energía en política exterior constructiva, bien podría reaccionar con agresividad internacional”.

Sin embargo, el republicano tendrá enfrente un Capitolio con ánimo de revancha tras dos años de desmanes y abusos de poder. “Un Congreso controlado por los demócratas podrá cuestionar las acciones del presidente en cada paso, ralentizando y tal vez deteniendo la constante expansión del poder ejecutivo desde el comienzo del segundo mandato de Trump y dificultando que un presidente posterior de cualquier partido siga los pasos de Trump”, señala William Galston, de la Brookings Institution.

La actitud desdeñosa de Trump con las elecciones es el resultado de su fracaso en la campaña electoral. A finales de septiembre, cuando las encuestas parecían sombrías para los republicanos, emprendió una frenética gira que le llevó a participar en mítines a lo largo del país. Visitó 30 Estados tratando de movilizar a sus seguidores. Pero sus votantes estaban frustrados por las promesas incumplidas por la guerra contra Irán y el consecuente encarecimiento de la vida.

Durante esas cuatro trepidantes semanas de campaña, el republicano pronunció discursos erráticos e inconexos en los que pasaba de hablar del conflicto en Oriente Medio al culo de Jon Husted, el senador republicano que buscó infructuosamente renovar su escaño. De proferir insultos a los demócratas —llamó yihadista al aspirante de Míchigan, Abdul El-Sayed— a, en un abrir y cerrar de ojos, pasar a alabar los atributos de la rapera Nicki Minaj.

Con 80 años ya cumplidos, los signos de cansancio iban apareciendo conforme avanzaba la campaña. Los bailecitos con los que divertía a sus simpatizantes eran cada vez más breves y su voz parecía cansada. Mientras, las encuestas no cambiaban la tendencia que auguraba una ola azul de costa a costa. Un escenario que ha acabado materializándose.

“¿Cómo hemos llegado hasta aquí?”, preguntó Trump a uno de sus colaboradores al final de la gira electoral, según el diario The New York Times.

Su decadencia a ojos de la opinión pública se inició casi al regresar al Despacho Oval. Maggie Haberman y Jonathan Swan cuentan en Regime Change, la obra que mejor describe los dos primeros años de su mandato, que Trump se sintió impune, sin reglas a las que ceñirse, tras salir indemne del juicio por el asalto al Capitolio del 6 de enero de 2021, cuando arengó a una masa enfebrecida para que impidiera la confirmación de la victoria de su rival Joe Biden en las presidenciales de 2020.

Así que cuando llegó a la Casa Blanca se sintió sin ataduras. A diferencia de su primer mandato, se rodeó de un equipo de fieles —y no de profesionales— que no osaban contradecirle. Al contrario, le animaban a ir más allá. Aprobó aranceles a diestro y siniestro, emprendió una guerra en Irán de la mano de Israel, desató la inflación y alentó negocios de su familia salpicada por acusaciones de trato de favor e información privilegiada, rompió la tradición para rediseñar los distritos electorales para sacar ventaja y se obsesionó con reformar Washington. Mientras, los estadounidenses percibían un reguero de promesas incumplidas que ha terminado por hundir su popularidad.

Agotado y decepcionado porque intuía el estrepitoso desenlace en las urnas, el lunes pasado, víspera de la votación, se desplazó desde la Casa Blanca al epicentro monumental de Washington para alardear de las obras del estanque reflectante del monumento a Lincoln. Unos trabajos a los que parecía haber dedicado más tiempo y esfuerzo que a resolver otros de los problemas acuciantes de los ciudadanos, como la crisis de la asequibilidad. En un extraño discurso, dedicó su último mensaje de campaña a resaltar el éxito de la reforma de la piscina reflectante.

Ahora, Trump está decidido a culminar su proyecto político y a completar su sueño de remodelar Washington a su imagen y semejanza, redecorando el Despacho Oval, inaugurando el salón de baile, levantando su arco del triunfo e intentando remodelar el Centro Kennedy.

La primera orden presidencial que aprobó tras las midterms da cuenta de ello. El jueves firmó una proclamación para designar el Despacho Oval, el Despacho Oval Exterior y el Salón del Gabinete de la Casa Blanca como monumentos nacionales.

“No se permitirá que nadie lo toque, lo destruya, lo derribe, gente estúpida, para construir algo con una forma ligeramente diferente. Es imposible que alguien destruya jamás este increíble espacio”, dijo a los periodistas, a pesar de que durante su estancia en la Casa Blanca ha sobrecargado las paredes con adornos y apliques dorados. También ha redecorado varias estancias, se ha cargado parte de la histórica rosaleda para construir un helipuerto e incluso ha derribado el ala este sin permiso del Congreso.

El viejo promotor de Queens, que pasó casi toda su vida peleando en el turbio mundo neoyorquino de la construcción, está dispuesto a librar la última batalla por preservar su legado. Aunque para ello tenga que sacar al diablo a pasear.

articles.body:
Qatar, the lead mediator in the US-Iran conflict, is seeking to persuade Tehran to allow UN nuclear weapons inspectors to visit Iran’s bombed nuclear sites, including those housing the country’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium.

Iran would not be required to make any commitment that the stockpile would be removed from the country, with other options on the table, including reducing the uranium content by down-blending it.

Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani, the emir of Qatar, spoke to Donald Trump about the proposal, the emir’s office said on Friday without revealing the call’s contents.

The state news agency said the emir “emphasised the importance of continuing dialogue and embracing diplomacy as a means of resolving disputes, preventing further escalation in the region”.

Trump is still considering whether to mount a further assault on Iranian nuclear sites, though the credibility of his threats is weaker inside Iran after his vice-president, JD Vance, said the war itself, and not just its cost to American consumers, was critical to the collapse of the Republican vote in the US midterms.

Under the Qatar proposal, the US would immediately lift the naval blockade on Iran in the strait of Hormuz and release a portion of the $8bn (£6bn) of its frozen assets. In return, Iran would agree to visits by International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors to its bombed nuclear facilities, based on a previous abandoned agreement that had been reached in Cairo in September 2025.

Iran would open the strait of Hormuz on the second day, via a route it has already negotiated with Oman that they would jointly lodge with the International Maritime Organisation (IMO).

Iran has multiple other preconditions for opening the strait including ending the war in Lebanon, a withdrawal of US forces from the Iranian coastline, a commitment to lift some economic sanctions, and agreement to pay war reparations. The sequencing of these commitments has been at the heart of the mediation.

In the memorandum of understanding, a $300bn reconstruction and development fund was to be set up to help Iran recover economically, but it was never clear exactly how this proposal was to be funded.

Iran, in a triumphalist mood after Trump’s election wipeout, has been wary of allowing the UN nuclear inspectors back into the country, claiming it had lost faith in Rafael Grossi, the head of the inspectorate.

Tehran claims Grossi betrayed his duty to uphold the nuclear non-proliferation treaty, by failing to criticise the US for bombing Iran’s nuclear sites. It fears that material gathered by the inspectors would be handed over as targeting data to the Americans and Israelis.

In the parallel talks on opening the strait, Oman’s foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi, spoke again to Iran about the future of the strait administration including the agreed route, the extent to which the agreement is temporary and the need to register the proposal with the IMO, either as a bilateral agreement or a joint regional proposal.

Oman has a long-term proposal for the administration of the strait compliant with the law of the sea in that shipping companies would be charged only for services, and not tolls.

Amir Hayat Moqaddam, the deputy chair of the Iranian parliament’s national security and foreign policy committee, told the Iranian Students’ News Agency (ISNA) on Tuesday that ships from four countries – China, India, Qatar and Iraq – were allowed to pass through the strategic waterway.

The exemptions served mutual interests, he said, adding that Iran charged Indian and Chinese vessels transit fees while allowing Qatari ships to pass free of charge. Medicine was received from India, while China provided political support.

It is reported that of the 10.23m barrels a day of Gulf crude that passed through the strait in October, about 42% went to China and 13% to India, said Muyu Xu, a senior crude oil analyst at the analytics firm Kpler.

The navy of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said two “violating” oil tankers attempting to pass through an unauthorised route in the eastern sector of the strait of Hormuz had collided with mines and caught fire.

The IRGC said the two tankers had turned off their navigation and identification systems and that the attempted crossing was with the support of US military forces.

articles.title: L'Iran: 'Esercito più forte dall'inizio della guerra'. Attacco 'rapido' Usa all'isola di Qeshm
articles.summary: Trump: 'Piccolo raid di pochi minuti'
articles.preview: L'esercito iraniano ha affermato oggi di essere "più forte" rispetto all'inizio della guerra in Medio Oriente, dichiarandosi pronto a rispondere a qualsiasi attacco in modo 'immediato' e "senza limiti geografici" a seguito delle recenti minacce statunitensi. "Le forze armate della Repubblica islamica sono oggi in uno stato di allerta più elevato e sono più potenti di quanto non fossero all'inizio della guerra", ha dichiarato il portavoce dell'esercito, Mohammad Akraminia, citato dall'agenzia ufficiale Irna.
articles.body:
L'esercito iraniano ha affermato oggi di essere "più forte" rispetto all'inizio della guerra in Medio Oriente, dichiarandosi pronto a rispondere a qualsiasi attacco in modo 'immediato' e "senza limiti geografici" a seguito delle recenti minacce statunitensi.

"Le forze armate della Repubblica islamica sono oggi in uno stato di allerta più elevato e sono più potenti di quanto non fossero all'inizio della guerra", ha dichiarato il portavoce dell'esercito, Mohammad Akraminia, citato dall'agenzia ufficiale Irna. "Su ordine della Guida Suprema, qualsiasi risposta delle forze armate sarà immediata, efficace e senza limiti geografici", ha aggiunto.

Nonostante i recenti attacchi statunitensi sull'isola di Qeshm, nello stretto di Hormuz, le trattative diplomatiche per evitare una ripresa delle ostilità si sono recentemente intensificate con la mediazione del Qatar, dopo una serie di minacce israelo-statunitensi.

L'agenzia di stampa semi-ufficiale iraniana Tasnim ha riferito che, secondo le prime segnalazioni, due missili avrebbero colpito l'isola di Qeshm, aggiungendo che non vi sono informazioni ufficiali su eventuali danni.

In precedenza, l'agenzia di stampa statale Irna aveva riportato la testimonianza di persone del luogo, secondo le quali due proiettili avrebbero colpito l'area di Suza, sull'isola di Qeshm, nel sud dell'Iran, dopo che era stato udito il rumore di un velivolo sopra l'isola.

"Non voglio parlarne. Abbiamo condotto un piccolo attacco in Iran. Hanno costruito un piccolo dispositivo antiaereo e lo abbiamo messo fuori combattimento in 15 minuti, forse cinque", ha detto Donald Trump, rispondendo a chi gli chiedeva se gli Stati Uniti fossero stati dietro l'attacco.

L'amministrazione Trump è spaccata sull'Iran. Il vicepresidente JD Vance preme per la fine del conflitto, mentre il capo del Pentagono Pete Hegseth e il numero uno dell'Us Central Command Brad Cooper spingono per un ritorno ai combattimenti. Lo riporta il Wall Street Journal citando alcune fonti, secondo le quali le tensioni fra le varie posizioni all'interno dell'amministrazione si sono intensificate dopo la elezioni di metà mandato.

I segretari di Stato Marco Rubio e del Tesoro Scott Bessent spingono invece per un inasprimento delle sanzioni e per proseguire il blocco. L'inviato Steve Witkoff sostiene la posizione di Vance. Il premier israeliano Benjamin Netanyahu vorrebbe una ripresa dei combattimenti. Gli Stati Uniti offrono 20 milioni di dollari, "oltre alla possibilità di trasferirsi altrove", a chiunque fornisca informazioni sul programma nucleare iraniano. Tali informazioni possono riguardare "le sue strutture, le sue attrezzature e il personale a esse associato", ha detto lo Us Central Command.

articles.body:
El 14 de mayo de 1964, a las 15.30, el señor Socker se presenta en el internado Monte Rosa de Montreux (Suiza) sin cita previa. Pide ser recibido por un asunto urgente. Es un tipo “simpático”, de mediana estatura, pelo negro peinado “a la moda”, y con un “excelente alemán”. A sus 33 años, dice ser estudiante en la Universidad de Jerusalén y miembro del Congreso Judío Mundial, pero “arrinconado” por las preguntas sobre su persona, admite ser del “servicio secreto israelí”.

Busca al criminal nazi Josef Mengele, cuyo sobrino estudia en el internado suizo. El informe policial sobre el intento de conseguir pistas en torno al paradero del macabro médico del campo de exterminio de Auschwitz, huido tras la II Guerra Mundial, concluye en un apartado de “características generales”, que Socker es un “mal mentiroso”, sin más. El supuesto espía fue despedido con una advertencia policial de no dedicarse a indagar más en Montreaux, según los documentos sobre el incidente, que forman parte de un archivo sobre Mengele del servicio de inteligencia suizo (NBD, en sus siglas en alemán) que no iba a ver la luz hasta 2071.

articles.body:
Donald Trump has said the US military on Friday carried out a new round of limited strikes on Iran, targeting an air defence system, describing the action as “minor.”

Iranian state media reported the sound of two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, which is in the strait of Hormuz, the crucial waterway for oil shipments that has been disrupted since the beginning of the US war on Iran in February.

In an exchange with reporters on Friday, Trump said “they built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five”.

The US military had previously reported carrying out what it described as “defensive” strikes on Monday, when explosions were heard on the islands of Qeshm and Hengam and in the nearby mainland area of Bandar Abbas.

Friday’s strikes are the first since Trump’s Republican party was dealt a stunning repudiation in Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US.

The electoral setback was stoked in part by voter dissatisfaction with Trump’s execution of the Iran war and elevated fuel prices – a byproduct of the war that has affected nearly every part of the global economy.

In the days since, Trump has vacillated between threatening to “destroy” Iran and suggesting a resolution to the war is near.

Differences with Iran about its nuclear program remain the thorniest issue and one that Trump insists must be resolved as part of any deal meant to end the war.

US Central Command, which oversees US military operations in the Middle East, announced in a post on X late Friday that the US was offering “a reward of up to $20m and possible relocation for information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community, or the movement of any of the above”.

The post included a link to the state department’s Rewards for Justice program.

Trump noted earlier Friday in an exchange with reporters that mediators’ discussions with Iran continue.

“We are talking to Iran. We have been,” said Trump.

A flurry of diplomatic phone calls in recent days between leaders in the Gulf and beyond has been aimed at easing tensions in the region. Concerns have mounted over the possibility that Trump could still order the US military to carry out new strikes against Iran.

US defense secretary Pete Hegseth spoke on Friday with his Qatari counterpart, Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, about developments, according to the Qatari government. Qatar has been mediating between the US and Iran to end the war.

The Qatari government announced the call between the countries’ defence officials after confirming earlier that Trump and Qatar’s emir had a separate call to discuss efforts to de-escalate tensions.

The telephone call between Trump and Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al Thani focused on international efforts to end tensions, according to a statement from the Qatari ruler’s media office.

With the Associated Press

European nations want Russia to halt its war against Ukraine before entertaining any talk of the Kremlin’s concerns about the continent’s broader security architecture, people familiar with the matter said, a stance that risks putting them at odds with the U.S. over the best way to end the conflict.

European officials are also adamant that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s pre-war demands that would effectively roll back NATO’s presence in Eastern Europe are still unacceptable, said the people, who asked not to be identified to discuss private deliberations.

One of the main goals of the existing security framework is to deter Russia from attacking Europe. It would make little sense to have such discussions while Moscow continues to wage war against Ukraine and is violating an array of existing agreements, some of the people said.

Activists used ladders to scale the perimeter fence and cut an opening to allow others inside. Some climbed a construction crane, displaying a banner reading "Fuck AI", while others waved Palestinian flags and held signs accusing Microsoft of supporting genocide. Police surrounded the protesters before the mayor ordered the demonstration to end. Riot officers subsequently intervened, with several arrests reported. The protest was organised by Dutch activist collective Geef Tegengas, alongside a separate mobilisation by environmental campaign group Fossielvrij NL. Campaigners oppose the development over its expected electricity consumption, its impact on housing plans and concerns about Microsoft's activities. The project, developed by Pure Data Centres for Microsoft, involves three towers approximately 85 metres high, with an investment exceeding $1 billion. Protesters argue that the facilities could consume as much electricity as all Amsterdam households combined, a claim that has not been independently established. The action formed part of an international campaign against large-scale data centres, with demonstrations planned across several European countries. Both Pure Data Centres and Microsoft said they respected peaceful protest, while urging demonstrators to avoid unlawful actions.

articles.title: UN says struggling to help millions fleeing Sudan war find shelter
articles.summary: The United Nations on Friday said about 15.4 million people who have fled conflict in Sudan need emergency shelter and essential household items, but humanitarian organisations are facing funding shortages.
articles.preview: Sudan Millions of people who have fled devastating conflict in Sudan face being left without shelter, the United Nations warned Friday. articles.body:
Sudan

Millions of people who have fled devastating conflict in Sudan face being left without shelter, the United Nations warned Friday.

After more than three years of civil war, the UN estimates that 15.4 million people need emergency shelter and essential household items.

But UN agencies said they had only been able to target 10% of those in need because of funding shortages.

And out of those, "we could reach only 900,000 people," said Mohamed Refaat, the International Organization for Migration's (IOM) chief of mission in Sudan.

The war raging since April 2023 between the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces and the regular army has killed more than 200,000 people, aid workers estimate, and has triggered the world's largest hunger and displacement crises.

Around 8.6 million people remain displaced within the country, millions have fled across borders and millions more have returned home — often finding houses, infrastructure and essential services damaged or destroyed.

Since the start of the year, Refaat said the UN agency had distributed more than 40,000 tents.

"But our warehouses are completely empty now," he told reporters in Geneva, speaking from Khartoum.

"We could soon reach a point where families desperately need shelter but there is simply nothing left."

In a joint statement, UNHCR and IOM said for those returning home getting help to find shelter "is often the first step towards rebuilding their lives".

But only one third of the $179 million needed this year to provide shelter has so far been funded, Abubakarr Jalloh, UNHCR's deputy representative in Sudan, told reporters.

Three in four internally displaced people in Sudan are women and children, Jalloh said, adding that El Niño-related weather conditions have made people more vulnerable because of significantly below-average rainfall across Sudan this year.

This has affected harvests in Darfur, Kordofan and other areas already devastated by ongoing fighting. Although food prices would normally ease after the harvest season, prices remain “painfully high,” the UNHCR official said.

“For a family that has lost everything, every Sudanese pound spent on food is money that cannot be spent on a blanket or on materials needed for safe shelter,” Jalloh stressed.

The agencies said less than half of the $2.9 billion needed for the overall humanitarian aid plan for Sudan had been funded.

articles.title: UNICEF: Children at risk of disease and violence from rise in attacks on water systems
articles.summary: Children around the world are at greater risk from disease, malnutrition and violence due to a sharp rise in attacks on water and sanitation systems. Now UNICEF is calling on conflict parties, governments and humanitarian actors to treat those systems as life-saving civilian infrastructure.
articles.preview: Children around the world are at greater risk from disease, malnutrition and violence due to a sharp rise in attacks on water and sanitation systems. articles.body:
Water

Children around the world are at greater risk from disease, malnutrition and violence due to a sharp rise in attacks on water and sanitation systems. Now UNICEF is calling on conflict parties, governments and humanitarian actors to treat those systems as life-saving civilian infrastructure.

According to a new report from the UN Children's Agency, attacks that damaged or destroyed water and sanitation systems in conflict rose threefold between 2021 and 2025.

That deprives children of safe drinking water and exposes them to disease from poor sanitation. The report also documents how children in Gaza have been killed or injured while queuing for water.

Longer more dangerous journeys also raise their risk of sexual violence and take time away from school.

Efforts need to be made to guarantee humanitarian access so that water and energy supplies keep running, UNICEF says.

It also calls for the protection of those who operate and maintain water systems and for all attacks to be systematically documented.

articles.body:
Czech arms makers look spaceward in bid to sustain Ukraine-driven boom

November 6, 2026

Czech arms makers have thrived on demand linked to the war in Ukraine. To sustain their growth, they need to look beyond ammunition and toward new technologies — and even space.

The Czechoslovak Group (CSG) arms maker announced in mid-October that it has acquired a stake in Canadian space technology manufacturer MDA Space.

This space mission is part of the company's bid to continue riding the boom that has transformed its fortunes in recent years.

When it listed on the Amsterdam Stock Exchange earlier this year, CSG soared to become the most valuable company in Central and Eastern Europe, with a market capitalization of €14.6 billion ($16.4 billion), propelling its owner, Michal Strnad, to the top of the region's rich list.

From 90s startup to major European player

CSG began life as a 1990s startup, selling military surplus amid the collapse of the Warsaw Pact, the military alliance between the Soviet Union and Europe's socialist Eastern Bloc nations, which was founded in 1955 and disbanded in 1991.

It has since grown to become the second-largest producer of ammunition in Europe after Germany's Rheinmetall and now produces across Europe and in the US.

The impact of the war in Ukraine

The main driver of the company's rising fortunes has been Russia's war in Ukraine, which has driven a dramatic boom across the Czech defense industry as a whole.

In 2021, the sector's exports totaled €600 million. In 2025, these exports had expanded to €4.7 billion, powered by orders placed by Kyiv and its European allies.

By the end of that year, European states had procured approximately €11 billion worth of military support for Ukraine from Czech defense firms.

Orders to the value of roughly €4 billion have arrived via the Czech Ammunition Initiative, a program that coordinates the transfer of artillery shells to Ukraine.

Amid the avalanche of orders sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, CSG and Czech peers such as STV, Colt CZ and PBS have been busy expanding production to pump out military vehicles and planes, guns, grenades, shells and bullets.

Historical link

"The war in Ukraine, particularly in its early stages, was especially well suited to Czech firms," Krzysytof Debiec of the Centre for Eastern Studies (OSW) told DW.

Debiec says that this was largely due to the major role that the former Czechoslovakia played in supplying Warsaw Pact countries.

"Specialization in the production of ammunition — including Soviet calibers — the repair of Soviet-era equipment and the manufacture of relatively unsophisticated systems that could be rapidly introduced and were compatible with the Ukrainian army's existing stocks," have all been key, he explained.

At the same time, European states eyeing the threat from the east and broader geopolitical instability are boosting their own defense budgets.

"The shift in US policies vis-a-vis NATO is forcing European nations to increase their defense spending dramatically, and that's another factor" in the Czech defense industry boom, Jan Jires, a former deputy defense minister and now a senior advisor at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, told DW.

Export dependence

However, since launching on the stock exchange, CSG's share price has performed erratically, illustrating the shifting sands on which Czechia's booming defense industry now stands.

The government in Prague has responded to the sector's surge by transferring the defense industry portfolio from the Ministry of Defense to the Ministry of Industry and Trade to align its growing role in exports with national economic and trade policy.

At the same time, the populist ruling coalition that took power a year ago is made up of parties that have either promised to lower support for Ukraine or — in the case of the far-right Freedom and Direct Democracy party (SPD) — are openly pro-Russian.

As a result, the coalition has halted contributions to the Czech Ammunition Initiative and is dragging its feet on raising defense spending to meet NATO targets.

This only limits an already small domestic market, leaving the industry dependent on exports for about 90% of its revenue — the vast bulk of which is still linked to Ukraine — and lacking a stable base for expansion.

"The Czech industry has outgrown the country's financial means," said Jires. "Unlike German, French or British companies, Czech manufacturers cannot rely on domestic demand to make them globally relevant."

What the future holds

Increased global defense spending looks set to continue, but an end to Russia's war in Ukraine, a change in US foreign policy or a calmer geopolitical environment would hit Czech arms manufacturers hard. For this reason, they must ponder what the future of war, and its funding, might look like.

The conflict in Ukraine offers some indicators, having become increasingly focused on swarms of drones and a technological race between Kyiv and Moscow to improve the performance of the unmanned aircraft.

Major questions must now be asked regarding "the size and role of the military, how it is equipped, what should be purchased and when new weaponry can arrive" Andor Sandor, a defense analyst and former commander of Czechia's Military Intelligence Service, told DW.

For a company like CSG, for which bullets and shells currently account for around 60% of sales, these are vital questions.

"Czech companies — many of which still focus on relatively unsophisticated military production — must invest more in innovative manufacturing," said Debiec, who notes that most are well aware of the challenge. "They have reinvested their extraordinary profits and are already more technologically advanced and diversified in their production than they were in 2022."

Space mission

CSG's acquisition of MDA Space is part of such efforts.

The company, which already held interests in British and German space technology companies, pointed to the close link between the space and defense industries when it announced the deal.

Noting that global government spending on space defense accelerated to €65.83 billion last year, CSG estimates that the overall space economy will triple in size to €1.6 trillion over the next decade.

Developing capabilities in space is "a natural extension" of its activities, the company stated, noting plans for further development in the segment, including a "dedicated space team."

To power such missions, Czech defense companies must make sure they're in a position to tap into funds for defense and space under the next EU budget, which could rise as high as €130 billion, said Jires.

"If they fail to do so, and all this money is grabbed by German, French and Italian companies," he warned, "Czech manufacturers may miss the opportunity to truly scale-up."
