articles.body:
November 6, 2026

Most people in Iran have little idea of the course of the US-led war and peace talks on the global stage. With few sources of information, the population must navigate conflicting rumors and fears of a nuclear attack.

"There is a constant sense of fear in the air," a 37-year-old mother in Tehran told DW. "Every time I hear a loud noise, I flinch. Even when a door slams, I jump — thinking that bombs are falling."

Now, unlike in the opening months of the war, her children are back at school.

"I don't work, but keeping the children at home out of fear is not a solution," she said. "They would go stir-crazy in our small apartment."

Iran's government takes aim at 'rumors'

Schools remain open across Iran despite the military standoff with the US and Israel. However, some parents whose children attend private schools have received messages from those schools explaining what to do in the event of a renewed war or other emergency.

Numerous parents have shared such messages on social media.

Irans Education Ministry has tried to reassure the public.

"People should not pay attention to rumors spread with the aim of sowing fear and forcing schools to close," Ali Farhadi, a ministry spokesperson, said in a recent media interview.

Farhadi said the ministry would decide whether the schools stay open or close, and would do so in coordination with the security authorities. Should the security outlook change, the situation will be reassessed accordingly, the official said.

'Pickaxe Mountain' at the center of nuclear attack fears

Parallel to Farhadi's appeal to disregard rumors aimed at raising fear, state media themselves are discussing scenarios of a possible nuclear attack.

On November 2, Iranian state television broadcast an advisory on protective measures in case of a nuclear strike. People were advised to remain in a shelter for at least 24 hours in the event of such an emergency.

Many in Iran fear that the United States is preparing to use nuclear weapons against the "Pickaxe Mountain" underground bunker about 220 kilometers (130 miles) south of Tehran. US President Donald Trump has hinted at attacking the location, which is close to Iran's Natanz nuclear facility, but made no explicit mention of using nuclear weapons.

Iran's government denies that any work related to its nuclear program is being carried out at the mountain bunker.

The fighting between the United States and Iran has mostly petered out in recent months as the Trump administration focused on the midterm election. But two days after the election, on November 5, the US news outlet Axios reported that the US military was making final preparations for a possible resumption of large-scale strikes against Iran.

Trump has 2 months before new Congress takes power

At the same time, there are also hopes that a Democrat-controlled Congress would force Trump to scale down his military ambitions.

"It is still difficult to make any concrete assessment of the implications of the US midterm election results for the war with Iran," Hamidreza Azizi, the International Crisis Group's consulting senior Iran analyst, wrote in response to questions from DW.

Iran's government sees the election results as a victory, Azizi wrote. The regime's resistance to the Trump administration has contributed to the Republican Party's loss in the US midterms, and some in Tehran are already seeking to frame the result as a sort of revenge for the US-Israeli assassination of senior Iranian leaders in the opening stages of the war.

Against this backdrop, Iran is likely to take an even harder line on its core demands.

Trump has at least two months before the new Congress takes office, Azizi wrote. He could decide to resume strikes on Iran in an attempt to offset a domestic political setback by targeting a foreign policy victory.

Reporters kept in the dark on peace talks

Qatari mediators are trying to persuade the Iranian and US governments to agree on a draft peace deal. The aim is to prevent another round of escalation and pave the way for the resumption of direct talks in the coming days.

But even well-connected journalists in Iran have little information on the substance of the talks, which are closed to the public.

In a post on X on October 31, the Iranian journalist Hadi Mohammadi wrote: "Domestic media outlets are completely in the dark about negotiations that directly affect people's everyday lives. They have to wait for reports from Axios, Al Arabiya, Al Jazeera and other international media outlets. In such an environment, developing our own narratives and doing journalism becomes pointless."

As the fog of war persists, many in Iran no longer have the energy to keep up with the media reporting. A 72-year-old retired woman from western Iran told DW she now deliberately avoids the news.

"I hardly have the strength to think about it anymore," she said. "I'm just glad that my three children have emigrated."

This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Taglia degli hacker sul dark web su Tajani e Lo Voi. Cyberattacco alla Galleria del Brennero
articles.summary: Solidarietà di Meloni al ministro. Il Ft: 'I servizi europei indagano sulla pista russa degli allarmi bomba'
articles.preview: Criminali informatici hanno diffuso dati personali sul dark web sia del ministro degli Esteri Antonio Tajani che dei sui famigliari. Lo ha reso noto lo stesso vicepremier su X. "Non mi farò intimidire in nessun modo", scrive. "Continuerò a lavorare per difendere il mio ministero e l'Italia, rafforzerò sempre più i legami e la collaborazione con i nostri alleati per proteggerci insieme. La nostra posizione sull'Ucraina è la ragione politica per cui sono entrato nel mirino.
articles.body:
Criminali informatici hanno diffuso dati personali sul dark web sia del ministro degli Esteri Antonio Tajani che dei sui famigliari. Lo ha reso noto lo stesso vicepremier su X.

"Non mi farò intimidire in nessun modo", scrive. "Continuerò a lavorare per difendere il mio ministero e l'Italia, rafforzerò sempre più i legami e la collaborazione con i nostri alleati per proteggerci insieme. La nostra posizione sull'Ucraina è la ragione politica per cui sono entrato nel mirino. Difendere la libertà di uno Stato sovrano, schierarsi in maniera limpida a favore di democrazia e indipendenza di una nazione per queste entità criminali è pericoloso". "Siamo di fronte ad una guerra ibrida, per questo ho chiesto al G7 che si svolgerà lunedi a Parigi di porre questo argomento al centro del nostro dibattito".

Secondo quanto scrive il Fatto Quotidiano sul darkweb, da almeno due settimane, gli hacker filorussi di "Noname057(16)" hanno pubblicato dati e richiesto notizie, a pagamento, oltre che sul ministro Tajani, sul procuratore di Roma Francesco Lo Voi e sul capo della Polizia postale Ivano Gabrielli. Sempre secondo il quotidiano questa minaccia ibrida è online perchè nessuno l'ha neutralizzata e sul caso indaga la procura di Roma.

E' dal 26 ottobre scorso che i NoName - che sono considerati legati al Gru (il servizio segreto militare di Mosca) - hanno inserito la 'taglia' sui dati sensibili di 18 persone, ritenute nemiche della Federazione Russa. Nel gruppo italiano, oltre a Tajani, Lo Voi e Gabrielli c'è Paolo Tassan-Zanin, sindaco di Aviano (Pordenone), sede di una base militare aerea americana.

Tra le personalità di spicco all'estero sono presenti Michael Schmid, presidente di Eurojust, Benjamin Krause, magistrato della Procura di Francoforte, Holger Münch, a capo della polizia criminale tedesca e Michael Alexander Martens, giornalista d'inchiesta ricercato da Mosca. Gli hacker offrono soldi in cambio di dati personali dei 'ricercati' e i profili di questi sono corredati da schede dettagliate con curriculum, dati pubblici, numeri di telefono privati, email e indirizzi civici delle abitazioni.

La solidarietà di Meloni a Tajani: 'Grande preoccupazione'

"Esprimo la mia piena solidarietà al vicepresidente del Consiglio, Antonio Tajani, per quanto emerso sull'attività di hacker filorussi e sulla diffusione sul dark web di dati personali che lo riguardano. La messa in vendita di informazioni riservate su esponenti delle istituzioni desta grande preoccupazione e va affrontata con la massima determinazione. Altrettanto preoccupante è la circolazione di immagini false, diffuse anche da esponenti dell'opposizione. La libertà di espressione non può mai diventare terreno di disinformazione". Così la premier Giorgia Meloni in una nota.

Cyberattacco alla società della Galleria del Brennero, indagini in corso. Isolati i sistemi interessati e avviate analisi forensi

Bbt Se (Tunnel del Brennero) è stata oggetto di un attacco informatico mirato, nel corso del quale soggetti non autorizzati hanno avuto accesso a dati accessibili tramite Internet, lo rende noto il quotidiano Tiroler Tageszeitung. La notizia è stata confermata all'ANSA da Bbt Se: "Non appena rilevato l'incidente, la società ha attivato i protocolli di sicurezza informatica, provvedendo all'immediato isolamento dei sistemi interessati e avvalendosi del supporto di specialisti esterni in cybersecurity per lo svolgimento delle necessarie analisi forensi. Sono stati avviati tutti gli adempimenti previsti e sono state informate le autorità competenti", informa Bbt. Sulla base delle informazioni attualmente disponibili, l'incidente non avrebbe avuto ripercussioni sulle attività operative della società. Sono tuttora in svolgimento approfondimenti per accertare i dettagli dell'attacco. Le indagini sono in corso.

L'attacco cyber, precisa Bbt Se - società europea per azioni, responsabile della progettazione e costruzione della Galleria di Base del Brennero - è avvenuto il 17 ottobre. Sono state tempestivamente informate le autorità competenti, le indagini sono state affidate alla polizia Postale di Bolzano e tuttora in corso. L'attacco avrebbe riguardato dati non accessibili al pubblico. La società dichiara che l'incidente non ha comportato, e non comporta, alcun rischio per i lavori in corso.

Resta ancora da chiarire l'effettiva profondità della penetrazione informatica e l'entità dei dati compromessi nell'attacco hacker che ha colpito la società di gestione Bbt Se. Sulla vicenda la società mantiene il massimo riserbo, evitando di commentare l'eventualità di trattative o il pagamento di presunti riscatti.

Come riportato dal quotidiano austriaco Tiroler Tageszeitung, a finire nel mirino degli inquirenti ci sarebbe il gruppo noto come 'Everest', riconducibile all'ambiente della cybercriminalità di lingua russa. Si tratta di una rete di estorsione internazionale specializzata nel furto di dati, nella minaccia di pubblicazione online e nella richiesta di denaro in cambio del silenzio. Il gruppo hacker inserisce il Tunnel del Brennero nella propria piattaforma dark web come obiettivo di attacco austriaco.

Il Ft: 'I servizi europei indagano sulla pista russa degli allarmi bomba'

Le agenzie di sicurezza europee stanno intanto indagando per accertare se le minacce di bomba coordinate che questa settimana hanno preso di mira decine di voli europei possano avere avuto origine in Russia. Lo riferisce il Financial Times, citando funzionari dell'intelligence secondo cui è in corso un'indagine transfrontaliera tra i servizi europei per risalire all'origine delle minacce.

Alcuni esponenti dell'intelligence europea ritengono che l'origine russa sia la più probabile, per movente, modalità operative, precedenti e primi indizi emersi. Un'ipotesi di lavoro è che le minacce siano di attivisti filo-Cremlino o gruppi hacker.

Sono complessivamente 35 i voli europei interessati da minacce di bomba nelle giornate del 3, 5 e 6 novembre, secondo il bilancio fornito all'ANSA dall'ufficio stampa di Eurocontrol, l'organizzazione europea per la sicurezza della navigazione aerea.

"Eurocontrol è a conoscenza di minacce di bomba contro 14 voli il 6 novembre, 14 voli il 5 novembre e 7 voli il 3 novembre 2026", precisa l'organizzazione chiarendo che il dato di ieri è ancora approssimativo. Il 6 novembre, a fronte di circa 29.550 voli nella rete europea, le segnalazioni hanno rappresentato lo 0,047% del traffico, contro lo 0,049% del 5 novembre, quando sono stati registrati 28.488 voli, e lo 0,026% del 3 novembre, quando i voli erano stati 26.278.

Gli allarmi "non hanno quindi avuto un impatto sui ritardi nella rete del traffico aereo", sottolinea Eurocontrol, precisando di monitorare la situazione e di lavorare "a stretto contatto con compagnie aeree, aeroporti, fornitori di servizi di navigazione aerea e altre organizzazioni in tutta Europa per limitare eventuali perturbazioni dei flussi di traffico aereo". Per le questioni relative alle minacce alla sicurezza, l'organizzazione europea rinvia alle compagnie aeree, agli aeroporti e alle autorità nazionali competenti.

articles.title: Why a new report on Anthropic automating AI development is alarming researchers
articles.summary: Anthropic is using AI to build more powerful AI. articles.body:
Anthropic is using AI to build more powerful AI. And it appears to be working remarkably well, with the company’s models improving roughly twice as quickly as a year ago, with little indication of slowing down.

AI is dramatically speeding up Anthropic’s research, even as the company calls for slowing down AI development.

That’s according to a new report published Thursday by the AI safety research organization METR, following an 11-week investigation inside the company, as part of a report evaluating its AI research and development. The probe is separate from a program offering safety researchers “employee-like” access to systems in the wake of high-profile hacking incidents over the summer.

The findings offer some of the clearest evidence yet of AI accelerating its own development, raising questions about how quickly the technology could advance toward a future in which AI systems can improve themselves with little or no human involvement. They also come at a pivotal time for Anthropic, which is preparing to go public even as its CEO, Dario Amodei, has publicly called for labs to pump the brakes on AI development.

But while the report offers a rare glimpse into the inner workings of the world’s leading AI labs, what it leaves out is just as revealing. Anthropic was permitted to redact portions of the final report as part of its agreement with METR, and it appears to have exercised that power liberally, raising questions about how much the public really knows about the pace — and risks — of frontier AI development.

Here are some of the biggest takeaways.

AI is dramatically accelerating Anthropic’s research and development

One of METR’s most noteworthy findings is that Anthropic’s AI models are improving roughly twice as quickly as they were a year ago, with benchmark scores suggesting “that Anthropic has made roughly two years of historical progress over the last year.” Crucially, METR’s researchers said they “are confident” that the acceleration was not simply due to scaling up the computing power used to train the models, which historically has been a major driver of AI progress.

Instead, the researchers said that the majority of the acceleration as of October “is due to AI,” with its contribution growing over time. That finding was supported by informal Slack polls and interviews with Anthropic employees, which pointed to sizable productivity gains. METR wrote that employees using Anthropic’s most capable internal model on average self-reported being around 12 times as productive at their respective work as they would have been without AI assistance, around double what staff had reported just a few months earlier while using Mythos 5.

For now, much of that acceleration appears to be coming from AI assisting human researchers, rather than AI working independently, though METR warned that “there are some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon.” Notably, the researchers said they found no clear signs of diminishing returns or observable bottlenecks that could prevent “even faster acceleration.”

Three of Anthropic’s newest AI models remain under wraps

Anthropic’s researchers are using more advanced AI models than the rest of us, with a lot of the acceleration and productivity gains described by METR attributable to unreleased internal models.

Over the past six months, Anthropic has finished training three models it has yet to release, according to METR. The pace of development is swift, with the models — codenamed Model 2, Model 3, and Model 4 — completing training in July, August-September, and September-October, respectively. METR also identified an unreleased model dating back to 2022, called Unreleased 2022. “These are the codenames shared with us; we understand they have different internal codenames,” the researchers wrote.

Anthropic is keeping key information secret

Anthropic gave METR access to a host of non-public information, including confidential research, model performance data, and employee interviews as part of the research process. It had no obligation to do so and by METR’s own admission, the AI lab “shared more information than was initially scoped for this project, surpassing our expectations.” This is commendable, but it is worth noting that Anthropic did not grant researchers unrestricted access, nor the kind of “employee-like” access it has promised other METR safety researchers as part of a separate program announced last month. It is an important distinction, given the reputational benefits companies can gain from independent assessments, even when they come with significant restrictions.

And there were significant restrictions. Anthropic had the power to redact information from METR’s final report — and it used that power extensively. “We submitted a ~100-page full report on our assessment to Anthropic. For the public version, Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative,” METR wrote on X.

METR reiterated those concerns throughout the report, highlighting other limitations on its access. “Our pipeline of information was relatively narrow, and a small number of our requests for data were denied.”

METR repeatedly stressed the impact Anthropic’s redaction decisions had on its ability to communicate its findings and for others to assess what’s going on at the company. It noted that much of the redacted evidence could have “multiple plausible interpretations,” making it difficult for the public to assess its findings, understand the uncertainties surrounding them, and judge the evidence themselves. “As a consequence [of the redactions], the public has to rely on METR’s judgment much more than would be ideal, given the weight of the questions answered here,” the report said.

In the report, METR said Anthropic justified the redactions on the grounds that releasing the information could benefit its rivals. However, METR said “most of the redacted information was very high-level,” even though it said it was not in position to comment whether redactions were justified commercially or not.

“We redacted a lot, and I accept that this makes it harder for others to check METR’s work,” Anthropic cofounder Sam McCandlish acknowledged in a lengthy post on X responding to METR’s findings. “But we determined that sharing exactly what is driving the speedup isn’t the right thing to do, both because it’s commercially sensitive and because it risks handing out a roadmap for others to go faster,” he said, adding that doing so would make the risks METR is concerned about “worse.”

McCandlish said that it’s a trade-off, but maintained Anthropic had made the “right call” in deciding to redact the information. He said the company plans to publish its own report on the speed of AI progress “in the coming weeks,” as well as new steps it’s taking to strengthen safety.

Anthropic is accelerating the very technology it warns is dangerous and faster than many expected

The publication of METR’s report has provoked a fierce backlash among AI safety researchers and commentators, largely centered on an apparent contradiction at the heart of Anthropic’s approach to AI: The company has been one of the most outspoken advocates for safety and responsible development, yet the report suggests it is helping accelerate the technology toward a threshold many consider dangerous, while seemingly failing to live up to its own commitments to transparency and accountability.

For some, the findings suggest that even many of the field’s most aggressive predictions about AI progress may be too conservative. They indicate that recursive self-improvement — AI systems that can autonomously develop increasingly powerful successor systems without human intervention, potentially accelerating development dramatically — may be closer than previously thought, raising concerns about whether existing safety measures can keep pace. While METR’s report only covers Anthropic, OpenAI said in September that it is “making strong progress” toward building an AI researcher that can “further progress on deep learning and alignment” by March 2028.

The report provides evidence about just how quickly AI is accelerating its own development

Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and founder of Apollo Research, which conducts AI safety testing for several leading AI labs, told The Verge the report suggests a pace of AI-enabled research and development even faster than what was forecast in AI 2027, an influential scenario that envisions a key breakthrough toward self-improvement in early 2027. He said the report has attracted so much attention because it provides evidence about something that has been very hard to pin down: Just how quickly AI is accelerating its own development.

Hobbhahn said the findings were broadly in line with what many in the field had expected, perhaps a little faster. Alan Chan, a senior research fellow at tech policy research center GovAI, told The Verge that the findings should prompt skeptics to reconsider their stance on AI accelerating AI development, and possibly shorten their timelines to when we will have systems that can fully automate tasks like software engineering.

On X, other researchers commented on the rate of acceleration and its implications for AI development. Sydney Von Arx, founder and CEO of AI safety organization The Nightingale Collective and a former METR researcher, also compared the findings to AI 2027’s timeline. Ryan Greenblatt, a METR researcher formerly of AI safety organization Redwood Research and one of three external researchers permitted to investigate OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face, said he “was seriously wrong about RSI speed up; I previously expected much less in 2026.”

Frustration is mounting over Anthropic’s approach to safety

Beyond highlighting the speed of AI development, the report has also fueled a growing sense of frustration over Anthropic’s role in driving that progress. The company has been one of the most vocal proponents of responsible AI development — and no stranger to calling for others to slow down — yet appears to be racing ahead itself. This report only builds on already heightened tensions from its IPO prospectus and future plans released last month.

Anthropic’s decision to heavily redact the report, citing grounds that revealing more could help its rivals accelerate their own development, has fueled accusations of hypocrisy. Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI researcher who now runs the AI Futures Project, which published AI 2027, accused Anthropic of “recklessly gambling with our lives,” adding that “it is pretty rich” of the company to cite others going faster as a reason to redact information when it does “not appear to be slowing down much at all.”

Anthropic declined to answer The Verge’s questions about the report and ensuing criticism, instead directing us to McCandlish’s post.

The redactions have also renewed calls for greater transparency and independent oversight of frontier AI labs, which grew to new heights earlier this year following a spate of incidents involving rogue AI agents. Brianna Rosen, research director for frontier security at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy, told The Verge that it was concerning that companies, not governments, were effectively calling the shots on automating AI research. “For democratic oversight to work, independent evaluators need the freedom to explain why they reached their conclusions, governments need to assess the evidence themselves, and the public has to trust this process,” Rosen said. “The report was not sufficiently transparent about the evidence.”

Pressure is building for more transparency from AI labs

Hobbhahn echoed Rosen’s concerns, saying that much of the reaction to the report stems from the apparent gap between Anthropic’s public safety stance and its actions. He pointed to the company’s decision to cancel part of the assessment designed to evaluate how much compute it allocates to safety work versus improving capabilities. METR said the company said “this was due to wanting to keep the engagement focused on risk assessment for the time being, and that it would revisit compute allocation verification later on.”

For Hobbhahn, the episode underscores the need for independent safety researchers to be embedded more deeply within AI labs, with significant access to internal systems and evidence. While his organization stands to benefit from such arrangements — Apollo is taking steps toward becoming an embedded evaluator at frontier labs — he is far from alone in calling for stronger oversight of AI development.

Others have called for more direct action. In a direct response to the report, New York state Assemblyman Alex Bores, a key figure shaping the Democrats’ AI agenda, called on Congress to “ban RSI, this year if possible.” With the blue wave of Democrats — many of whom campaigned against AI companies — taking office soon, the prospect of tougher restrictions is a very real possibility.

And with AI research showing little sign of slowing down, the pressure is set to intensify. Hobbhahn said he had another takeaway from the report, too: “Brace for craziness,” he said. “It is going to go very fast,” likely way too fast for society or politics to keep up.

The threats against Tajani, who is also vice prime minister of Italy, come amid a spate of hoax bomb threats across Europe that have forced flight diversions, security alerts at broadcasters, and attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems.

“They are also targeting my family; they are willing to pay for more details about me and my loved ones,” Tajani added in his X post. “My response is very simple: I will not be intimidated in any way.”

‘Matter of grave concern’

Meloni expressed solidarity with Tajani “following the revelations about the activities of pro-Russian hackers, and the publication on the dark web of personal data”.

She called attempts to sell confidential information about government officials “a matter of grave concern that must be addressed with the utmost determination”.

Tajani added in his statement that Italy’s “position on Ukraine is the political reason I have been targeted: defending the freedom of a sovereign state, taking a clear stand in support of a nation’s democracy and independence, is dangerous in the eyes of these criminal entities”.

He also suggested that the cyberthreats may also be a reaction to the Italian government’s efforts to strengthen the Foreign Ministry’s digital defences.

Tajani did not specify what kind of information had been shared, but suggested that the cyberthreat was ongoing.

He added that the ministry was taking the threats seriously and was coordinating its response with allied countries.

“Large-scale and strategic investment support measures are essential for establishing a domestic semiconductor supply chain,” Takaichi said at the meeting.

The 28 priority items were picked from 62 products and technologies in 17 strategic fields. They are expected to have significant economic spillover effects.

The government will formulate an implementation plan by the end of the year, designating the next five years as a period for intensive investments.

The priority items include vertical and physical AI, data centers, biopharmaceuticals, quantum computing, shipbuilding, and the refining of critical minerals.

CEO Sam Altman said recently that OpenAI is prioritizing safety instead of going ‘guns blazing’ toward an IPO.

Echoing FT and Wall Street Journal reports from last week, Bloomberg says OpenAI is still pursuing additional investments that could increase the amount to $20 billion, and that it had initially hoped to raise as much as $30 billion at a higher valuation of $1.4 trillion. That was before tech stocks dropped, and the results of the midterms showed how much public opinion has turned against AI companies and data center projects.

OpenAI’s rival Anthropic filed its S-1 to go public last week. Earlier this year, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said it’s holding off on its own IPO until it can make more confident claims about its models’ safety. He didn’t give a specific timeline for the IPO, but said at the time, “I think it’s also kind of bad for the world if OpenAI waits too long to go public.”

OpenAI previously intimated that it would go public this year but subsequently delayed its plans. There are expectations that the company will IPO next year at some point.

The market for AI hangs in a particularly precarious place. The Democratic landslide in the U.S. midterms — and overwhelmingly negative voter sentiment around data centers — has caused jitters throughout the market, with many anticipating potential regulatory challenges in the future.

articles.body:
Batteries are everywhere, even on the battlefield, which helps explain the Pentagon’s recent interest in building more domestic manufacturing capacity.

The 12-year-old, North Andover, Massachusetts-based startup 6K announced Thursday that it won conditional approval for a $250 million loan from the Department of Defense to build a factory in Tennessee. The plant will use a unique microwave-powered process to produce battery materials that don’t rely on Chinese suppliers.

The company previously received a $50 million grant from the Department of Energy under the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, though that 2023 grant was canceled by the Trump administration in a chaotic sweep of Biden-era awards, forcing 6K to reapply.

The factory was originally slated to open in 2024, but the grant cancelation and uncertainties in the EV market forced the company to rejigger its plans.

6K’s manufacturing process uses microwaves to heat metals into a plasma and then deposit them onto a surface, reducing the number of steps required to make cathode material, a key battery component. The company says the process can work on a number of different battery types, including lithium iron phosphate (LFP).

articles.title: Japan launches emergency cybersecurity package after wave of attacks
articles.summary: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the package includes security countermeasures, strengthening of investigation systems and reinforcement of support for victims and measures to prevent the spread of damage.
articles.preview: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the package includes security countermeasures, strengthening of investigation systems and reinforcement of support for victims and measures to prevent the spread of damage. TOKYO: Japan launched a multimillion-dollar emergency policy package on Friday (Nov 6) to address a sudden wave of hacking incidents. The country's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has vowed to take action after dozens of businesses reported unauthorised access in recent weeks to their systems and potential leaks of client data.
articles.body:
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the package includes security countermeasures, strengthening of investigation systems and reinforcement of support for victims and measures to prevent the spread of damage.

TOKYO: Japan launched a multimillion-dollar emergency policy package on Friday (Nov 6) to address a sudden wave of hacking incidents.

The country's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has vowed to take action after dozens of businesses reported unauthorised access in recent weeks to their systems and potential leaks of client data.

Hacks and data breaches have ballooned worldwide, with AI's ability to find previously unknown ways to break into computer systems in the global spotlight.

"In light of the current situation involving increasingly serious cyberattacks, all ministers present today have put their heads together to formulate an 'emergency countermeasures package,'” Takaichi told her ministers on Friday.

The package would initially be funded by 10 billion yen (US$63 million) available in the government's budget but the overall cost would likely be higher, with the premier asking her finance minister to figure out how to free up funds for the entire plan.

The package includes security countermeasures partly through the use of AI, strengthening of investigation systems, and reinforcement of support for victims and measures to prevent the spread of damage, she said.

Media reports have said the package includes the creation of a "cyber rescue team" made up of both government and private sector experts.

The government will set up a secretariat within the current fiscal year to coordinate the deployment of the rescue team when support needs are particularly acute, the Yomiuri Shimbun daily, Jiji Press and other reports said.

Takaichi did not mention the cyber rescue team but said that mobilisation was needed to "keep up with the speed of cyberattacks in the AI era.

"Even at this very moment, incidents of unauthorised access and information leaks are occurring one after another, having a major impact on the lives of our citizens and on corporate activities," she said.

"Let us mobilise the full capabilities of the government to strengthen our nation’s overall capacity to respond," she added.

Chinese artificial intelligence cybersecurity tool Artex was used in several recent hacks of Japanese companies, an information security arm of Japanese IT firm GMO Internet Group Inc said last month.

GMO Internet Group itself is among those that have come under attack.

articles.body:
Hackers behind the $6.3 billion theft from Binance Holdings are moving some of the stolen cryptocurrency through Chinese money-laundering networks, according to blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis.

The hackers, identified by U.S. authorities as members of North Korea’s TraderTraitor group, have been seen transferring stolen assets through thousands of digital wallets and across multiple blockchains in an effort to obscure their origins. North Korean hackers are said to have used Chinese money-laundering networks in previous thefts as well, and Chainalysis said that it’s tracked hundreds of thousands of dollars from the Binance theft — a fraction of the total stolen — flow into these networks.

The flows into money laundering networks, which include over-the-counter trading desks, suggest that hackers are pushing to take funds off of blockchain networks and cash them out, said Chainalysis.

articles.title: North Korea's army of world-class hackers is secret weapon that took down Binance
articles.summary: North Korea identifies top students from a young age, training a select few for cyber operations and rewarding them with perks such as spacious apartments and huge hard currency awards, defectors and analysts say.
articles.preview: North Korea identifies top students from a young age, training a select few for cyber operations and rewarding them with perks such as spacious apartments and huge hard currency awards, defectors and analysts say. SEOUL: North Korea rewards its top hackers, tasked with heists like the Binance crypto hack that netted US$6.3 billion, with perks such as a spacious apartment in the capital of Pyongyang and huge hard currency awards, despite gruelling hours of work.
articles.body:
North Korea identifies top students from a young age, training a select few for cyber operations and rewarding them with perks such as spacious apartments and huge hard currency awards, defectors and analysts say.

SEOUL: North Korea rewards its top hackers, tasked with heists like the Binance crypto hack that netted US$6.3 billion, with perks such as a spacious apartment in the capital of Pyongyang and huge hard currency awards, despite gruelling hours of work.

Leader Kim Jong Un has assembled an army of world-class hackers using such incentives in a programme more than a decade old that picks 200 of the smartest middle school students each year to study computer engineering, defectors and analysts say.

A fraction eventually become hackers in an investment that has paid off dramatically, as the group has evolved from the early days when it ran illegal gambling websites to pulling off the world's biggest cyber heist last month.

"They are actually one of Kim Jong Un's secret weapons," said Kim Heung-kwang, a North Korean defector who trained hackers of behalf of the state before fleeing to South Korea in 2004.

"There is no other country grooming hackers like this, systematically searching for the smartest children, solely to turn them into operatives," he added. "Whether they want to be a hacker or not does not matter."

The FBI and Binance have said North Korea was responsible for the Binance hack, but Pyongyang has denied that. Blockchain investigation firms have attributed it to a North Korean group known as "TraderTraitor".

The denial is part of a pattern in which the North dismisses such blame over the years as fabricated political provocations.

SYSTEMIC SELECTION

North Korea set up a cyber unit in 1998 but elevated its status after Kim came to power and declared in 2013 that cyber warfare was, along with nuclear weapons and missiles, an "all-purpose sword" crucial to the country's strike capability.

Candidate selection begins in middle school as early as 11 or 12 years of age, with authorities picking about 150 to 200 children a year to study computer science, said Kim Heung-kwang, the former trainer, and two defectors who worked in IT.

At 17, the top performers are sent to North Korea's best universities and undergo further screening before a chosen few finally enter the military's cyber unit as hackers, they added.

They are trained in areas such as cryptocurrency protocols and reverse-engineering foreign hardware devices in addition to more conventional topics such as advanced mathematics and foreign languages, one of them said.

Those who do not become hackers are trained to turn out software or apps for Western firms via remote jobs.

"While South Korea's best students may pursue medicine or other prestigious careers, North Korea channels top talent into nuclear and cyber programs and essentially guarantees their future," said Lim Jongin, professor emeritus at the school of cybersecurity at Korea University.

Other privileges on tap for the hackers are travel abroad to allied countries, such as China, where they can more freely access the internet.

Successful exploits can earn as much as 30 per cent of the heist's profits in US dollars for the hackers' military unit, and they can even receive a flat in the capital where their parents can also stay, Kim said.

"There are accounts that successful cyber personnel are given apartments in Pyongyang," Lim said, adding that the flats could range to as much as 1,420 sq ft.

Such performers are also eligible for membership of the ruling party and high-status marriages into elite families, said one of the defectors.

But it is a small group. The North's cyberwarfare operations employ about 8,400 people, South Korea's National Intelligence Service estimated in 2024.

North Korean state media do not publicly celebrate such hackers' achievements, but they regularly highlight students who show talent for programming.

In 2015, North Korea opened the Mirae Scientists Street in the capital, in the construction of which Kim Jong Un had been closely involved, state media said.

Hackers' formal designation in the North was "scientist" or "researcher", said one of the defectors.

STATE ADVANTAGE

Other hacking groups associated with North Korea include the Lazarus Group, also known as APT38, which the US accused in 2022 of having stolen hundreds of millions of dollars worth of cryptocurrency from the Ronin blockchain network. The FBI has said TraderTraitor is affiliated to Lazarus.

State backing makes the North's hackers more dangerous and harder to repulse, as they face no consequences for hack after hack, enabling them to perfect their strategies, analysts said.

"In the world of cyber crime, often, if you make a mistake ... that is all law enforcement needs to get you," said Alec Zebrick, senior manager for Asia-Pacific global services at Chainalysis.

But North Korea's hackers "are doing this for the regime, so they're going to continue, even after successes", he added.

"Even after failures, they'll continue, because it's very hard for the international community to take action against them."

Other groups that have engaged with North Korea IT workers who earn funds for the Kim regime by landing remote technology jobs at Western companies describe them as highly organised, polite in their interactions and avid users of AI.

"There clearly was a structure you would see in military. Strict times, cleaning boots, very orderly," said YouTuber Deeveeaar, who has claimed to have hacked into cameras watching North Korean IT workers at their jobs.

"To say they 'use a lot of AI' is an understatement. AI is the very backbone of their operation," he said, citing use of paid ChatGPT accounts, Claude Code and Cursor, among many AI tools.

"They write code with it, alter their resumes and help make new ones. And even forge documents and identities."

Binance said the hackers used a bogus job interview and software hidden in an advertisement to compromise staffers' computers before using an internal AI tool to seize control of systems.

In 2025, a sanctions monitoring team drawn from 11 United Nations members said TraderTraitor had obtained both ChatGPT and DeepSeek accounts.

TOUGH WORKING CONDITIONS

Yet the lifestyle of a hacker or elite technology worker for North Korea is gruelling, particularly when given a mission or sent abroad, say former IT workers and human rights groups.

Living in cramped spaces, often working stretches longer than 10 hours a day, constant surveillance and strict targets are among the downsides, said former IT workers interviewed for a report last year by advocacy group PSCORE.

"There is always pressure to keep earning money," said the group's executive director, Nam Bada. "The stress is extreme, and because of the psychological strain people develop health problems they didn't have before."

IT workers must meet a monthly target in dollars, or face humiliation and other punishments, he said.

Still, the hackers' success is likely to embolden the North Korean leader as they get better and grow more ambitious, analysts say.

"We see more and more them leaning towards what we call 'big game hunting'," said Zebrick.

"So they're targeting some of these larger organisations, potentially have larger vaults of funds, that they could potentially get. These are harder targets," he added.

"However, as we can see with the Binance case, the payout certainly can make it worth their time."

articles.body:
Secondo la confederazione, nel terzo trimestre 2026 la spesa per l’elettricità sostenuta dalle imprese del terziario ha raggiunto i 3,8 miliardi di euro, mentre quella per il gas si è attestata a 788 milioni

Gli aumenti delle bollette energetiche continuano a colpire duramente le imprese del terziario, con effetti sempre più pesanti sui costi di gestione e sulla competitività. A lanciare l’allarme è Confcommercio: secondo le stime dell’Osservatorio Energia della confederazione (OCEN), nel terzo trimestre del 2026 la spesa per elettricità e gas sostenuta dalle attività economiche del settore ha subito un’impennata a causa dei rincari delle quotazioni energetiche internazionali.

La spesa per l’elettricità

Nel terzo trimestre del 2026 - come denuncia l’OCEN - la spesa per l’elettricità a carico delle attività del settore è aumentata del 46,2% rispetto allo stesso periodo dello scorso anno e del 66,4% sul trimestre precedente, raggiungendo la cifra totale di 3,8 miliardi di euro.

La conseguenza è stato un evidente rincaro sulla bolletta media mensile, che ha sfiorato, complessivamente, i 29.700 euro. Sono stati colpiti in modo particolarmente duro bar (+133%), alberghi (+68%) e grandi superfici di vendita (+67%).

Il costo del gas

Anche sul fronte del gas Confcommercio rileva una situazione di forte criticità, con aumenti record: nel terzo trimestre la spesa complessiva delle imprese del terziario si è attestata a 788 milioni di euro, il 72,7% rispetto al 2025. La bolletta media mensile, invece, ha superato gli 11mila euro, per un aumento complessivo del 66,9% su base annua.

La ragione degli aumenti

A monte delle bollette sempre più salate, secondo Confcommercio, ci sarebbe la nuova impennata dei prezzi dell’energia sui mercati globali, che a inizio novembre hanno raggiunto i massimi dell’anno. Il petrolio Brent ha superato i 100 dollari al barile, registrando un aumento tendenziale del 69,4% a ottobre, mentre il gas al TTF di Amsterdam è salito a 96,3 euro/MWh (+173,4% su base annua).

articles.body:
A Pordenone chiusa la terza edizione della fiera promossa dalla Regione Autonoma Friuli Venezia Giulia - Realizzati oltre 260 incontri B2B

Con un bilancio di oltre 260 incontri B2B, pianificati tramite agenda digitale fra le imprese espositrici e le aziende della tradizione, ha chiuso la terza edizione di Eureka, Fiera per le Imprese Culturali e Creative promossa a Pordenone Fiere dalla Regione Autonoma Friuli Venezia Giulia.

È stata una opportunità di crescita e uno spazio concreto di business matching nel quale aziende ad alta innovazione e imprese del comparto manifatturiero e industriale hanno potuto dialogare e stringere nuove collaborazioni commerciali. Un circolo virtuoso che ha coinvolto anche brand nazionali, da Fincantieri (con Marine Interiors) a Crédit Agricole, intorno al tema sempre più importante dei Talenti Creativi in azienda.

«La due giorni - spiegano gli organizzatori - ha dimostrato nei fatti che inserire stabilmente designer, artisti ed esperti di storytelling all’interno delle divisioni strategiche e dei processi di Ricerca e Sviluppo permette alle aziende tradizionali di affrontare con maggiore competitività le complesse sfide dei mercati del nostro tempo». Eureka è l’unica vetrina nazionale dedicata alle Imprese Culturali e Creative: al centro dell’attenzione l’impatto macroeconomico della Creative Economy, settore capace di attivare un impatto complessivo di circa 310 miliardi di euro sull’intera economia nazionale, indotto incluso.

«La Regione Autonoma Friuli Venezia Giulia, che si distingue a livello nazionale per essere stata tra le prime amministrazioni a misurare scientificamente l’impatto economico della cultura sul Pil regionale, pari nel 2025 a oltre 2,1 miliardi di valore aggiunto, riafferma così la propria visione di “cultura di frontiera” – ha detto il vicepresidente della regione e assessore alla Cultura e allo Sport Mario Anzil - Un’infrastruttura strategica e un motore concreto di sviluppo in grado di valorizzare il capitale umano e alimentare la solidità della produzione industriale italiana sui mercati globali».

Una conferma «della capacità di Pordenone Fiere di essere non solo luogo espositivo, ma piattaforma di incontro tra competenze creative e sistema produttivo. Integrare creatività, innovazione e manifattura significa generare nuove opportunità di business e rafforzare la competitività delle imprese», ha spiegato il presidente di Pordenone Fiere Renato Pujatti.

articles.body:
Bank of Japan Gov. Kazuo Ueda said that while his nation’s inflation rate has reached policymakers’ target, it’s unclear how long it will stay there, and indicated it hasn’t yet become embedded among the broader Japanese public.

“Underlying inflation is 2% — our goal is to keep it there,” Ueda said in a question and answer session after delivering a speech at the International Monetary Fund in Washington on Friday. “I think we are in equilibrium,” he said. “Whether we could stay in that equilibrium for a very long time to come, we still don’t know.”

The remarks come a week after the BOJ marked a milestone by declaring that underlying inflation had reached the bank’s 2% target for the first time since the goal was introduced in 2013. Ueda didn’t offer any specific guidance on the central bank’s appetite to raise interest rates further, in an exchange with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva.

Hakeem Jeffries, the leader of House Democrats, promises to “stop the stupid Trump tariffs jacking up prices on Americans.” Ron Wyden, incoming Senate Finance Committee chairman, says he’ll reassert congressional authority over trade policy. Even Senator Ted Cruz, the Texas Republican, lamented that “tariffs have made everything too expensive.”

But curbing President Donald Trump’s tariff powers won’t be easy or quick, and there’s a risk any efforts to do so in the incoming Democratic-led Congress will spur infighting in both parties.

While the president tempered his policies ahead of Tuesday’s election, he has several potential trade barriers in the pipeline. Trump could announce a new set of duties linked to excess industrial capacity that would hit imports from more than a dozen economies — even before Democrats take control in January.

Presentata la nuova edizione davanti a 600 studenti. Percorso con 50 parole chiave. Lagarde (Bce): «Grazie all’Osservatorio per il suo lavoro sull’alfabetizzazione economico-finanziaria»

Capire l’economia e la finanza per scegliere il futuro. Young Factor Europe porta l’educazione economico-finanziaria nelle scuole superiori di sei Paesi, con una piattaforma gratuita e un percorso costruito su 50 parole chiave. Andrea Ceccherini, fondatore e presidente di Osservatorio for Independent Thinking, ha presentato la nuova edizione a Milano davanti alla presidente Bce Christine Lagarde e a 600 studenti.

Ceccherini: «Esercizio per partecipare alla vita democratica»

La posta in gioco supera la gestione dei risparmi: «Studiare la finanza e l’economia – spiega Ceccherini – è oggi un esercizio per partecipare a pieno titolo alla democrazia». Quello dell’alfabetizzazione economico-finanziaria,ha commentato la governatrice della Bce, è «un tema che mi sta particolarmente a cuore e che considero una componente essenziale della libertà: in particolare per le donne, conoscere gli strumenti finanziari e disporre delle competenze necessarie per gestire le proprie risorse significa poter compiere scelte autonome e decidere del proprio futuro». Da qui il «ringraziamento» all’Osservatorio per l’alto valore civile dell’iniziativa e «per il lavoro che sta facendo».

Le Cinquanta parole

termini Il progetto è in fase pilota avanzata in Italia, Germania e Spagna e avviata in Francia, Paesi Bassi e Portogallo. Nel nostro Paese il progetto è sostenuto da Intesa Sanpaolo e UniCredit ai quali si aggiungerà anche Crédit Agricole Italia.

Il fulcro sono 50 parole, spiegate e illustrate, che si affrontano in cinque anni: test per misurare le conoscenze, videolezioni, attualità, masterclass dei governatori delle banche centrali e attività pratiche. A disposizione di docenti e studenti il giornalismo di Financial Times, The Economist, Wall Street Journal e Sole 24 Ore, attraverso la piattaforma Doubt and Debate.

Lagarde: «Questioni finanziarie ancora poco capite»

Quanto sia necessario questo alfabeto lo indica la stessa Lagarde parlando davanti agli studenti a Milano: in Europa, osserva, «il 50% dei cittadini ha una comprensione molto limitata delle questioni finanziarie. C’è chi fatica a distinguere un tasso fisso da uno variabile». Lacune che si riflettono sulla capacità di valutare un’offerta, gestire le proprie risorse e decidere con consapevolezza.
